item.title: Jordan Love wins fifth career NFC offensive player of the week award
item.description: Jordan Love has been outstanding throughout the 2026 season, but he had an especially strong game against the Patriots on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Jordan Love has been outstanding throughout the 2026 season, but he had an especially strong game against the Patriots on Sunday.

Now the Packers’ quarterback has been named offensive player of the week for the first time in 2026.

Love finished the 45-27 victory 23-of-29 passing for 372 yards with three touchdowns and zero interceptions. He also had a rushing touchdown.

Love’s 153.2 passer rating was No. 1 in the league for Week 9 and his 372 passing yards along with a 79.3 completion rate led the conference.

This is the fifth career offensive player of the week award for Love, who last won it for his Week 13 performance last season.

Love and the Packers will host the division-rival Vikings in Week 10.

item.title: Jaguars designate DE B.J. Green for return
item.description: The Jaguars have welcomed three new players to the team this week and they will also be reintegrating a current member of the team into practice.
item.content:encoded:
The Jaguars have welcomed three new players to the team this week and they will also be reintegrating a current member of the team into practice.

The team announced on Wednesday that they have designated defensive end B.J. Green for return from injured reserve. Green suffered an elbow injury in the first game of the season.

Green played three special teams snaps in that game. He joined the Jags as an undrafted free agent in 2025 and appeared in 14 games. He had 15 tackles, two sacks and a fumble recovery.

The Jaguars will have a 21-day window to activate Green and he'll be ineligible to return this season if he does not rejoin the active roster before that period is over.

item.title: Seahawks swap practice squad defensive tackles in lone trade deadline day move
item.description: Seattle’s quiet trade deadline featured a minor practice squad transaction.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks’ deadline day move was on the margins.

The Seahawks signed defense tackle Cole Brevard to their practice squad, they announced on Tuesday. In a corresponding move, fellow defensive tackle Gary Smith III was released to make room for Brevard’s addition.

After going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft, Brevard signed with the Kansas City Chiefs as a UDFA and spent training camp and preseason with the team. After he was waived during the cuts from 90 to 53, he was briefly signed to the Chiefs’ practice squad but was released ahead of the start of the regular season.

A six-foot-three, 346-pound nose tackle, Brevard began his college career at Penn State but appeared in just one game as a freshman. He spent the next three seasons at Purdue, where he played 37 games and totaled 38 tackles, 5.5 tackles for loss, and 2.5 sacks. He closed out his collegiate career at Texas, posting 18 tackles and one TFL.

item.title: Titans sign LB Mohamoud Diabate off Panthers practice squad
item.description: The Titans have added a linebacker.
item.content:encoded:
The Titans have added a linebacker.

Tennessee announced on Wednesday that the club has signed Mohamoud Diabate off of Carolina's practice squad.

Diabate was with the Titans earlier in the year, spending the offseason and training camp with the club. He was on the practice squad and appeared in one game before being released from the unit late last month. He then joined the Panthers’ practice squad.

Diabate spent the last three seasons with the Browns, appearing in 46 games with 18 starts.

In all, Diabate has recorded 128 total tackles with eight tackles for loss, three passes defensed, and a forced fumble.

item.title: Dolphins sign Keith Cooper Jr. to replace injured Zach Sieler
item.description: Cooper Jr. was signed off of Carolina Panthers’ practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins announced yesterday that veteran defensive tackle Zach Sieler would miss the remainder of the 2026 season due to a biceps tear he suffered against the Detroit Lions last Sunday. On Wednesday, the team made a move to replace their defensive lineman.

Miami signed Keith Cooper Jr. off of the Carolina Panthers’ practice squad. The move immediately places Cooper on Miami’s 53-man roster.

Here’s what Miami’s official website had to say about Cooper.

“Cooper Jr. has appeared in four career games with Cleveland (2025) and Miami (2026), recording one tackle. He first joined the Dolphins on Jan. 9, 2026, and spent the first three weeks of the season on Miami’s active roster. Cooper Jr. entered the NFL as an undrafted college free agent with Detroit in 2025 and spent time on the practice squad with the Lions and the Browns. He finished his collegiate career at Houston (2024), where he started 12 games and recorded 46 tackles (25 solo), 3.5 sacks, 8.5 tackles for loss, two passes defensed and one fumble recovery. He transferred to Houston from Tulane following the 2023 season after appearing in 39 career games with 15 starts and recording 73 tackles (37 solo), 10.5 sacks, 16 tackles for loss, five passes defensed and one forced fumble in three seasons (2021-23) with the Green Wave.”

item.title: Tom Brady offers high praise for Drake Maye despite rough Patriots loss
item.description: Brady called Sunday’s Patriots vs. Packers game for Fox.
item.content:encoded:
New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye did not play his best game Sunday with Tom Brady back at Gillette Stadium.

With Brady calling the game from the broadcast both, Maye threw three interceptions in the Patriots’ 45-27 loss to the Green Bay Packers. Despite the rough outing, the former Patriots quarterback remains impressed by what he has seen from Maye throughout his young career.

“Been absolutely terrific,” Brady said on the Fox broadcast. “To come in here in his first year, it was a totally different offense and it didn’t really showcase what his abilities were. Then he got Josh McDaniels in his second year who is really teaching him the cerebral part of the game. He’s orchestrating the line. He’s orchestrating the protections and the run games. Over the last two years I see the maturity. I see the willingness to know when he can change a play and when he can’t. And just his overall expectation for himself all the time.”

After a rookie season in which Maye started just 12 games, the quarterback took a significant Year 2 leap when paired with offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels.

Maye went on to break Brady’s single-season franchise record with a 72% completion rate while throwing for 4,394 yards and 31 touchdowns. He finished second in MVP voting and led the Patriots to the Super Bowl.

His third season has featured more ups and downs. Following a slower start, Maye had operated as one of the NFL’s best quarterbacks over the five weeks leading into Sunday’s matchup with Green Bay. While his overall performance has been less consistent this season, Brady has continued to notice his growth within the offense he spent much of his career in.

“When Josh would normally just bring in the game plan, he would just kind of go, ‘Hey, this is what we’re running.’ Now Drake Maye is like, ‘No, no, no, how about we put this guy in this spot and this guy in this spot?’” Brady said. “There’s much more ownership from Drake Maye. That’s the cerebral part of the game, when you have this type of quarterback that thinks his way through the game, you’re going to see a progression over time of that play continue to get better and better and better.

“I know today has been a rough game obviously with the interceptions, but he’s had a hell of a young career.”

item.title: Colts mishandled the Jonathan Taylor situation
item.description: When the dust settled on the trade deadline, the Colts still had running back Jonathan Taylor under contract.
item.content:encoded:
When the dust settled on the trade deadline, the Colts still had running back Jonathan Taylor under contract. It was not the outcome that most around the league expected.

All signs pointed to the Colts taking the best offer at 3:45 p.m. ET and processing the paperwork before the top of the hour. Whatever the best offer was.

But that's what a functional organization would have done. The Colts currently are not.

The Giants were willing to give up a second-round pick and a fifth-round pick for Taylor. It's unclear for now whether anyone else was willing to do better than that.

In the interim, Taylor spent two weeks not knowing what would happen. He didn't get an assurance he wouldn't be traded until roughly an hour before the window closed. (Even then, the leak felt more like a "last call" to interested suitors.)

The fans spent that same period of time wondering what the Colts were doing. And Taylor got only eight carries in the 42-7 loss to Jacksonville, at a time when it felt like a trade was imminent.

So what happens next for Taylor? If they try to trade him in the offseason, they won't do better than they would have done when a contender was willing to pay a premium in an effort to win now. And if they don't get at least as much as they could have gotten on Tuesday, will they refuse to trade him again?

Taylor could end up being stuck on the Colts during an obvious rebuild. Then, by the time it's rebuilt (if it ever is), Taylor will be past his prime.

The simplest explanation is that the Colts slipped into dysfunction on this one. And it's no surprise. Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon is still fairly new to the job. The G.M. has been fired. And coach Shane Steichen hopes to win enough games to have a chance to keep his job; he surely wasn't lobbying to lose his best player.

So what should the Colts have done? When they were doing the deals for guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, they should have asked for the various Taylor suitors to make their last, best offers. And the Colts should have made a final decision then and there as to whether he'd be traded or retained.

Instead, they decided to wait and see whether the offers would improve. Taylor was left to wonder about his future. After the Week 9 loss to the Cowboys, he basically said goodbye to Indianapolis.

The Eagles didn't play it that way with running back Saquon Barkley. They knew what was out there, they decided not to take the best offer, and they informed Barkley that he wouldn't be changing teams.

The Colts instead kicked the can, not accepting the best offer and hoping it would impove. That gave Taylor two weeks to ponder the possibility of playing for a contender before the Colts decided not to pull the trigger on a trade.

They'll never admit it, but the Colts will come to regret not taking the best deal. Because the offers won't get any better after the season. At some point, Taylor is going to realize it's in his best interests to request a trade.

That will be a problem for the next G.M. to deal with. And that wrinkle won't make the job more attractive to a candidate who has options.

item.title: Orange in the NFL: week 9 update
item.description: Get your McCord jerseys before Sunday
item.content:encoded:
Each week we want to give you an update on former Orange in the NFL. Let’s get to this week’s recap of the 9th week of the NFL season and at least one former Orange on the move at the trading deadline

Arizona Cardinals: Garrett Williams

Williams played special teams in Arizona’s loss to Seattle.

Atlanta Falcons: Matthew Bergeron

Bergeron was Atlanta’s highest rated offensive player according to PFF with an overall grade of 80.3 and a run blocking grade of 90.9.

Cleveland Browns: Andre Szmyt

Szmyt hit all three of his field goal attempts against the Saints. He’s now 19-21 on the season for the Browns.

Dallas Cowboys: Justin Barron and Alijah Clark

Barron and Clark both saw time on special teams in the win over the Colts.

Detroit Lions: Jackson Meeks

Meeks didn’t play against Miami and now he’s a victim of Orange on Orange crime.

Green Bay Packers: Zaire Franklin

Franklin missed the game against the Patriots due to injury.

Houston Texans- Jawhar Jordan

Jordan remains on the practice squad in Houston.

Jacksonville Jaguars: LeQuint Allen and Trebor Pena

Allen saw snaps on offense and special teams but didn’t record any stats in the win over the Ravens. Pena remains on the practice squad.

item.title: AP Chiefs Mailbag: Is Josh Downs more of the same in KC’s WR room?
item.description: Arrowhead Pride staff writer Jared Sapp answers your questions after Kansas City returns to the win column.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag!Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs!

The Chiefs beat the New York Jets in virtually every aspect of the game in Sunday’s 35-12 victory. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds with a new weapon joining the team for Week 11.

Swaf asks:


Josh Downs. A 5’9″ 170-pound small WR. Is this what the Chiefs really need at WR? He was held without a catch on Sunday. Sounds familiar to me. I just don’t think another small WR is the answer.

Downs definitely has a body type that many Chiefs fans are tired of, but he also plays the role the Chiefs envision much better than the other options they have gone through since Tyreek Hill left town in 2022. Downs isn’t a project where there is a major question about how he will fit or what he can do in the NFL. This is a player who has racked up 2494 receiving yards over three and a half seasons. When he joins the team on Wednesday, he will walk into the room as the most accomplished member of Kansas City’s wideouts.

The 2023 third-rounder has proven himself apt in the catch-and-run situations that make Kansas City’s offense go. What is encouraging is that he has been better on deep routes in 2026 than in his first three seasons. His average depth of target (ADoT) in 2026 is a career high of 9.5. He will not be Tyquan Thornton, but there may be a little downfield action to further unlock with him.

Throughout his career, Downs has generally played bigger than his size and has only missed three games in his career. He probably isn’t the superstar we continually ask Kansas City to add, but he should greatly raise the floor of the offense even as he works his way in over the next few weeks.

PettyMahomes asks:


Is there any sense that Josh Simmons will play this year? The o-line is terrible and needs a big infusion of talent.

Rarely does a player put themselves into head coach Andy Reid’s doghouse as Simmons appears to have done. Once those players play themselves out of the team’s plans (such as cornerback Marcus Peters or wideout Kadarius Toney), there isn’t a great track record for making their way back into the team’s good graces.

I do not have any inside information. If I had to guess, I would fathom that Simmons never playing for Kansas City again is a more likely outcome than playing in 2026. I definitely hope that I am wrong. Certainly, the ability to play a position at a level that is almost impossible to acquire outside of a top ten draft selection could see Simmons given another opportunity.

If there is another chance for Simmons to get back onto the field, I would watch for the weeks leading up to the Week 14 game against the Cincinnati Bengals, when Kansas City will come off of a mini-bye after consecutive Thursday games.

I don’t think anyone is counting on Simmons, and any contribution would be seen as a pleasant surprise.

KCDane asks:


Why aren’t offensive and defensive line part of the trade needs and discussions before deadline?

The Chiefs appear set to get a front seven reinforcement back in second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott, who seems on the verge of returning from last season’s ACL tear. Perhaps Norman-Lott is activated ahead of Sunday’s road contest with the Atlanta Falcons. His 21-day practice window to come off of the Physically-Unable-to-Perform (PUP) list will expire before Week 12’s game against the Arizona Cardinals.

The Chiefs’ priority truly needs to be to get Norman-Lott back in the fold while working with rookies R Mason Thomas and Peter Woods to improve over the season’s second half rather than rental players.

We will see if Simmons presents a similar opportunity to add a player from within the system this season. Even so, the league-wide supply of starting tackles is so thin that such players are rarely available at the trade deadline. Even if teams fall out of contention and shift the focus to evaluating in-house talent, the offensive line has to hold up to make any real conclusions about players in question.

If the Chiefs had touched another position group besides wide receiver, I would have liked to have seen them add a safety or coverage linebacker with a proven history of matching up with tight ends.

BuckeyeChief asks:


Is there any chance the AFC West leading Denver Broncos stumble? For a hot minute, I thought the Carolina Panthers might sneak by and get a win on them, but that didn’t happen. Many are saying that the AFC West title is already lost for the Chiefs, but like Lee Corso says, “not so fast, my friend.”

It’s going to be hard to catch the Broncos based on remaining schedules. Simply put, Denver’s schedule is significantly easier the rest of the way than Kansas City’s.

The Broncos certainly aren’t perfect, and their dependence on second-half comebacks — as against the Chiefs and Panthers the last two weeks — will probably fail them once or twice. I won’t be surprised if the teams finish with the same record and with 5-1 division records.

One result that could prove unfortunate for Kansas City if tiebreakers go to common opponents is losing to the Seattle Seahawks while the Broncos were able to come out on top of them. Kansas City would do well to win against the Los Angeles Rams as Denver did. Beating the San Francisco 49ers (who handed Denver their second loss) would also greatly help Kansas City’s case.

Both the Chiefs and the Broncos have the Buffalo Bills and New England Patriots remaining on the schedule.

There is still much football to be played, and sometimes teams just don’t finish the season as strong as expected. The division should not be written off for Kansas City. For it to happen, the best thing would be simply to keep winning — while holding our noses and cheering on the Las Vegas Raiders when they travel to Denver in Week 11.

OzarkEd asks:

Will we play a complete game from start to finish this season?

The Jets possessing the ball for so long on their first two drives (resulting in field goals) probably gave Sunday’s game more of a sour note than the performance deserved. Momentarily fearing that Patrick Mahomes needed Tommy John surgery also did not help.

A better start would have been great, but I’d call that a pretty complete game, overall.

The Chiefs won 35-12, scoring five touchdowns without allowing one and shutting out an opponent in the second half. New York never advanced past the Chiefs’ 22-yard line after halftime. Kansas City outgained New York 391 yards to 229, even with the game ending almost evenly split in time of possession. The pass rush even came to life, delivering five sacks.

Perhaps the Chiefs can get off to a faster start in one of their next two games against opponents who have probably moved into player evaluation mode. But it’s hard to control a game against any opponent like Kansas City did in Week 9.

Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! We will be back after the Chiefs try to keep the winning going in Atlanta. Keep watchingThe Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

item.title: Cam Heyward says Mike Tomlin is still coaching him up from a distance
item.description: Mike Tomlin still has an impact on the Steelers defense in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers selected Cameron Heyward with the 31st overall pick in the 2011 NFL Draft. His 16 seasons with the franchise make him the team’s longest-tenured player. However, when Mike Tomlin stepped down from his position as head coach of the franchise in January, even the Steelers’ most experienced veteran would be in uncharted waters with a new head coach in 2026.

Fast forward to November of the 2026 season, and the Steelers are in first place in the AFC North with a 6-2 record under Mike McCarthy. However, Tomlin’s fingerprints are very much all over this team in more ways than one.

On his “Not Just Football” podcast, the Steelers veteran defensive lineman opened up about Tomlin’s impact on the players this season through a group chat.

“He’s been texting me all season long,” Heyward admitted on his Not Just Football podcast. “Week in and week out, about different defensive linemen. Who we about to play. It’s me and T.J. together. There’s a crazy group chat going on right now.”

Tomlin acknowledged that the group chat is an example of how much he cares for the success of Heyward and Watt as they continue their careers without him leading the charge.

“Our relationships are real,” Tomlin said. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the jobs we hold. I love these dudes, man. I care about these dudes, and I wanna see them be successful. And so, sometimes wanting to see them be successful and saying some things that aren’t necessarily nice, but I’m hoping they get it from somewhere else.”

Heyward later revealed that Tomlin texted the group chat after their Week 8 win over the Cleveland Browns to thank them for doing their job and picking up the win. Even though he isn’t coaching anymore, Tomlin still has hate in his heart for the Steelers division rival.

Tomlin always had the reputation of being a “players coach” and someone that players around the league would want the opportunity to play for. Getting to hear stories from Heyward about how Tomlin continues to push him and talk to him speaks to how special their relationship was and still is.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Eagles-Giants Film Review: Tired of trying to find reasons to be interested in an offense that keeps failing in the same ways
item.description: All-22 analysis from Philadelphia’s Week 9 loss.
item.content:encoded:
What else is there to say about this offense? I keep sitting down to write these reviews hoping that the film will give me something different to discuss. Instead, the Eagles ended up with 220 yards of offense, 13 first downs, and an average of 3.3 yards per play. They had the ball for nine and a half fewer minutes than the Giants. Another week, another miserable offensive performance. Hooray!

Joe Milton gave us a few things to enjoy. His mobility prevented an already awful performance from looking even worse, and there were a couple of throws that showed why his arm talent is intriguing. But changing the quarterback hasn’t changed how I feel watching this offense. It is still boring, disjointed, and far too difficult. At this point, I want this staff to move on so I can start looking forward to a new season. It’s November! I’d like to feel excited about the Eagles’ offense again.

Anyway, there are still individual players to evaluate and specific problems to explain. Let’s get into it.

Offense

Welcome to the Eagles’ offense, Joe Milton! No surprise, but play action under center doesn’t work as the pressure arrives before he has a reasonable opportunity to do anything. We have seen versions of this all season. Putting a different quarterback behind it doesn’t make the protection work.

The Eagles use a four-man slide to the left, leaving Markel Bell isolated on the right. That gives the edge defender a two-way go against a rookie tackle who has struggled. Meanwhile, the tight end helps on Jordan Mailata’s side. I understand that protection calls have rules, but surely those rules should help you account for your personnel? If I am going to spend a tight end on a chip, I would rather have him help the rookie right tackle than my franchise left tackle. Bell still has to execute his assignment, but the staff could make that assignment more manageable.

Milton’s scrambling was one of the few reasons this game remained watchable. On this play, there isn’t a great option unless you expect him to fire the quick out into a tiny window from the opposite hash. He creates something with his legs, which is a useful skill when the passing concept gives him so little. I struggle to imagine what the offense would have looked like without those quarterback scrambles.

The rushing numbers show how much he was covering up. Remove all quarterback runs, including scrambles, and the Eagles’ running backs finished with 16 carries for 28 yards. 1.75 yards per carry. The 92-yard team rushing total makes the run game look considerably more functional than it was because the quarterback could move.

I rarely criticize a quarterback simply because a screenshot shows somebody open. Route concepts have progressions, and a receiver looking open doesn’t automatically mean the quarterback should have been looking at him. Even so, it is pretty remarkable that Milton doesn’t spot Makai Lemon completely uncovered in the slot here. There is nobody there! That is an opportunity you would want your quarterback to recognize.

The Eagles ultimately benefit from defensive pass interference on the throw to Darius Cooper, so the result is successful. The process still frustrates me. Once again, an answer to pressure is to give an outside receiver a one-on-one opportunity and ask him to win. I can live with that more easily when the receiver is prime A.J. Brown. Especially with a new quarterback, I would like the offense to provide a more accessible answer than repeatedly asking for a difficult individual win on a deep shot.

Hey, an actual creative run call! The touchdown uses Willie Lampkin as a fullback, with Tyler Steen pulling on power. Fred Johnson is also out there. So the Eagles use 7 offensive linemen! Lampkin does a good job leading the way; Steen does a great job pulling. This was a nice example of using the players available to create a different picture for the defense. More of this would have been welcome.

What frustrates me is how rarely that creativity travels beyond the goal line. Why can’t Lampkin get some opportunities at fullback elsewhere? They don’t need every run to look like this. But when the usual approach produces almost nothing, trying more of what worked seems reasonable. What exactly have they got to lose? Who doesn’t want to see more Lampkin right now?

The extra-lineman Jumbo packages were probably my favorite part (the only part I enjoyed) of the offensive plan. They didn’t work on every snap, but they provided a minor spark to an offense with nothing else. Fred Johnson gives the Eagles a better blocker than the tight ends they keep asking to handle difficult assignments. Outside of Dallas Goedert, those tight ends rarely feature in the passing game anyway. If the additional eligible receiver isn’t threatening the defense as a receiver or helping enough as a blocker, what is the benefit of keeping him out there?

The Eagles ran four designed runs with Fred Johnson as an extra lineman. Those gained 12 yards and included the touchdown above with Lampkin also eligible. There was enough here to justify exploring it further, because as you will see later, it helped the pass game. I would rather see the Eagles give Johnson more work than keep asking Johnny Mundt, Grant Calcaterra, and Eli Stowers to make a run game function through blocking assignments they aren’t winning.

We talk about the details every week because the details keep being poor. Here is mesh, a concept designed to create traffic through crossing routes and make it hard for defenders to track receivers crossing the formation. Except the Eagles appear unsure about who is supposed to create that traffic for the cornerback covering Lemon. Nobody does it.

The protection doesn’t give the play much chance anyway. Landon Dickerson loses immediately, which has become a serious problem. I thought he showed some better things in the run game against the Cowboys, but his pass protection remains a major concern. He was bad. We can acknowledge his injury issues and still recognize that what is happening on the field is not good enough.

The blitz operation remains a mess. My best guess is that Milton is supposed to be hot here, meaning he has to get the ball out to account for a defender the protection cannot block. But I don’t know the Eagles’ exact rules. What we can see is an offense that still doesn’t look coordinated when the defense brings pressure. That has been happening long before Milton got here.

The condensed alignments make this harder. This is so obvious to me, but the team keeps doing it. Bringing the receivers close to the formation also brings their defenders closer to the quarterback and gives a cornerback a much shorter path when he blitzes. That can be worth the tradeoff if the offense uses the alignment well and has clear answers. Too often, the Eagles appear to invite pressure without making the defense pay for it. Spread the formation occasionally. Make the corner show his intentions or travel farther. Give the new quarterback a picture he can manage. Something has to become easier.

For all that, Milton did produce a couple of throws I enjoyed. This is a dime. He subtly shifts left in the pocket and delivers the ball with excellent placement. Lemon does his part, settling into the available zone and catching the ball away from his frame. Good stuff! I would have liked to spend considerably more of this review discussing plays like this.

Milton finished 18 of 34 for 169 yards, with no touchdowns or interceptions, so this wasn’t a good overall passing performance. But individual moments still matter when evaluating someone making his first start for the team. He showed the ability to move and deliver a quality ball. Markel Bell’s get-off is also worth watching on this clip. He frequently leaves his stance slowly, and it looks like there may be a snap-count issue. Whatever is causing it, he needs to get moving sooner. Starting late makes difficult pass-blocking assignments even harder.

This game was death by 2×2 passing concepts. Two receivers on each side isn’t inherently a problem, obviously. The problem is what the Eagles kept doing with it: too many hitches, too little downfield stress, and very little combination of horizontal and vertical stretch. The defense wasn’t consistently being forced to cover enough space or make difficult choices. So many of the concepts felt like variations of this.

The numbers fit what I saw. The Eagles used 2×2 on 25 dropbacks, their most-used passing formation. Those plays included 20 attempts, two sacks, and three scrambles. Milton completed 12 passes for 117 yards, but the EPA per dropback was minus-0.233, and the success rate was only 24%. Roughly one in four dropbacks generated positive EPA. That’s rough.

Drew Kendall also needs to handle this rep better. He doesn’t look prepared for the linebacker coming and gets driven straight back into the quarterback. I have liked aspects of Kendall’s development, but this wasn’t his best game, and Bell struggled again too. For a team that needs young offensive linemen to become part of the solution, that is worrying. Outside of Mailata, how many players on this line do you currently feel good about moving forward?

I haven’t included many running plays because there is only so much you can say about repeated failure. The offensive line didn’t generate enough movement, and the Eagles continued to condense the formation despite their receivers and tight ends struggling as blockers. Tight splits don’t magically create a good run game. You still need the players at the point of attack to execute, and the structure needs to match what they can do.

On this play, they manage to leave a defensive tackle unblocked. Dickerson doesn’t rescue it by picking up the blitzing linebacker, either. It is another snap where the whole operation breaks down badly enough that discussing the runner feels almost pointless. These are the mistakes that should have been addressed months ago. How is the offensive line coach still here? I don’t expect every young player to win every rep, but I do expect the unit to understand who it is blocking. That is a basic part of preparing an offense.

The jumbo play-action passes were a welcome exception. Watch the defense respond to the run threat here. The extra offensive lineman gives the Giants something they actually have to respect, and that response helps create space for Goedert. This is why personnel and the run-pass relationship matter.

On the two passes explicitly marked with Johnson eligible, Milton went two-for-two: 15 yards to Lemon and 19 yards to Goedert. Including the four designed runs and one scramble marked with Johnson eligible, those seven plays produced 47 yards. It is a small sample, but it was one of the few approaches that gave the offense useful production through the air and on the ground. Why didn’t we see more of it? If the tight ends aren’t creating a credible run threat, using an extra lineman gives you a way to change that picture. It’s pretty striking to watch the Giants respond to play action when the Eagles have a 6th offensive lineman, compared to what has happened most of the season.

Milton still left opportunities on the field, and this miss is frustrating precisely because he’s such a talented thrower. Goedert is available up the seam, but Milton doesn’t step into the throw, and the ball has no juice. This should have been a substantial completion. The arm is more than good enough to make it, but the delivery doesn’t give the play what it needs.

Sometimes gifted throwers can get away with inconsistent fundamentals because they have enough arm to compensate. I can’t tell you why Milton delivers this particular ball the way he does, but having a huge arm doesn’t remove the need to set up and finish the throw properly. The offense gave him plenty of problems he couldn’t solve. This was an opportunity he could have taken. Both things can be true. Evaluating him fairly means acknowledging the good throws and the frustrating misses.

Lemon finished with six catches for 61 yards and led the Eagles in receiving. There were good moments, including the zone catch earlier in the thread. But he also had two bad drops, and this final-drive miss is one he has to make. There is room to turn upfield and then try to get out of bounds. The Eagles probably still don’t win, but catching it at least gives them a chance to keep the drive moving.

One of Lemon’s biggest selling points coming out of USC was his hands. He isn’t a big receiver or an explosive vertical threat, so reliability on these opportunities has to be part of his value. I am not going to turn one game into a sweeping verdict on a young player, but if drops start creeping into his game, I will be disappointed quickly. This is supposed to be his bread and butter.

Final Thoughts

Milton made a few plays, and I am looking forward (somewhat) to watching him again. His scrambling created yards the offense wasn’t producing by design, and some of his throws were fun to watch. The jumbo packages also offered something the staff could build on.

But I am tired of trying to find reasons to be interested in an offense that keeps failing in the same ways. The protection is rubbish, the run game barely functions, and too many passing concepts make the defense’s job incredibly easy. The players aren’t executing well enough either, but the staff has had all season to improve the operation. We are still discussing the same problems.

I don’t have a new dramatic conclusion this week. I want this staff to move on. I want something new and an offense that gives me something to look forward to. Right now, watching this team feels like waiting for something to end.

Thank you for reading! I’d love to hear your thoughts, so feel free to comment below and ask any questions.If you would like to support me further, please check out my Patreon here!

item.title: Here we go again: Can Houston’s 3–5 start spark another playoff run?
item.description: Houston’s been here before. The Texans are ready to make their run.
item.content:encoded:
At this exact point in time last season, the Houston Texans were 3-5 coming off a gutsy loss to the 6-2 Denver Broncos. Both seasons have been filled with optimism and frustration, criticism and accolades, clumsy losses and big wins. Texans fans are well aware of what happened last year; they went on a nine game winning streak to close out the season and secure the fifth seed in the AFC Playoffs. The question is, can they do it again?

This article will compare the Texans current situation in the AFC South, AFC, and remaining schedule through Week Nine of the NFL season against last year’s team.

2025 AFC South Standings through Week Nine

  1. Indianapolis Colts: 7-2
  2. Jacksonville Jaguars: 5-3
  3. Houston Texans: 3-5
  4. Tennessee Titans: 1-8

2026 AFC South Standings through Week Nine

  1. Jacksonville Jaguars: 6-2
  2. Houston Texans: 3-5
  3. Indianapolis Colts: 2-7
  4. Tennessee Titans: 1-8

In theory, Houston is in a much better place in the AFC South than last year. While the Colts were predicted to come back to earth, no one would predict they wouldn’t miss the playoffs entirely. Given both the Jags and Colts were playing such good football, winning the division was out of the question.

The Jags play the Titans two out of the next three games and also have Dallas (4-5), Washington (2-5-1), and Indianapolis (2-7) on their schedule. That’s five easy victories to get them to 11 wins. Catching Jacksonville may once again not be feasible. They’re currently the most efficient offense and most dominant defense in the league statistically. With Houston three games back from the Jags, it makes more sense to evaluate their place in the AFC.

2025 AFC Playoff Picture after Week 9

  1. Indianapolis Colts (7–2, 6–1 AFC)
  2. New England Patriots (7–2, 4–2 AFC)
  3. Denver Broncos (7–2, 4–2 AFC)
  4. Pittsburgh Steelers (5–3, 4–1 AFC)
  5. Buffalo Bills (6–2, 4–1 AFC)
  6. Los Angeles Chargers (6–3, 5–1 AFC)
  7. JacksonvilleJaguars (5–3, 3–1 AFC)
  8. Kansas City Chiefs (5–4, 2–3 AFC)
  9. Houston Texans (3–5, 2–2 AFC)
  10. Baltimore Ravens (3–5, 2–3 AFC)
  11. Cincinnati Bengals (3–6, 3–2 AFC)
  12. Las Vegas Raiders (2–6, 2–4 AFC)
  13. Cleveland Browns (2–6, 1–4 AFC)
  14. Miami Dolphins (2–7, 1–6 AFC)
  15. New York Jets (1–7, 1–4 AFC)
  16. Tennessee Titans (1–8, 0–7 AFC)

2026 AFC Playoff Picture after Week 9

  1. Buffalo Bills (7-1, 4-1 AFC)
  2. Denver Broncos (7-2, 3-1 AFC
  3. Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2, 5-2 AFC)
  4. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2, 3-2 AFC)
  5. Kansas City Chiefs (6-2, 6-1 AFC)
  6. Cincinnati Bengals (6-2, 4-2 AFC)
  7. New England Patriots (5-4, 5-1 AFC)
  8. Cleveland Browns (5-4, 3-3 AFC)
  9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-5, 3-3 AFC)
  10. Baltimore Ravens (4-5, 2-4 AFC)
  11. Houston Texans (3-5, 3-3 AFC)
  12. New York Jets (2-7, 2-4 AFC)
  13. Indianapolis Colts (2-7, 1-5 AFC)
  14. Miami Dolphins (1-7, 1-4 AFC)
  15. Tennessee Titans (1-7, 1-5 AFC)
  16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-8, 0-5 AFC)

Visually, the Texans occupy a more precarious position within the conference than they did at this juncture last year.Statistically, however, they remain right on track. The AFC boasts a combined 65 wins through this point in 2026—identical to its total at this exact stage in 2025. Among the current top seven playoff seeds, the numbers mirror each other precisely as well: 43 combined wins for the conference’s current postseason field.

Houston faces four remaining games against opponents with superior records. At this time last year, that figure stood at five. That represents one fewer hurdle where the Texans can directly alter the postseason race by knocking off an established contender.

While the exact trajectory of the remainder of the season remains unwritten, expecting a repeat rescue via total collapses from the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs is a statistical long shot. Still, the path forward relies entirely on self-execution rather than outside charity.

Given the current playoff race mirrors last year’s the magic number to make the playoffs is 11. That means Houston has to go 8-1 to earn a Wild Card spot. With games against the Packers, Jags, and gritty Browns, there’s little room for error. The Texans schedule has eased up a bit with the Ravens, Commanders, and Eagles all struggling thus far.

2025 Houston Texans Remaining Schedule after Week 9

vs Jacksonville Jaguars (5-3)
@ Tennessee Titans (1-8)
vs Buffalo Bills (6-2)
@ Indianapolis Colts (7-2)
@ Kansas City Chiefs (5-4)
vs Arizona Cardinals
vs Las Vegas Raiders (2-6)
@ Los Angeles Chargers (6-3)
vs Indianapolis Colts (7-2)

2026 Houston Texans Remaining Schedule after Week 9

@ Cleveland Browns (5-4)
vs Indianapolis Colts (2-6)
vs Baltimore Ravens (4-5)
@Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2)
@ Washington Commanders (2-5-1)
vs Jacksonville Jaguars (6-2)
@ Philadelphia Eagles (2-7)
@ Green Bay Packers (6-3)
vs Tennessee Titans (1-8)

Houston benefitted from playing almost an exclusive slate of AFC opponents down the stretch. Their wining streak helped bring them into the Wild Card race by defeating their rivals for those final few spots. The Texans playoff hopes aren’t in their hands. Just like last year, they need several teams to collapse to make way for their run. A Lamar Jackson-less Ravens team, a Steelers team who hasn’t faced much competition, and a young but unproven Browns team all are prospective teams to fall a part down the stretch. Even then, Houston would still be only eighth in the AFC. To make it to the playoffs for the fourth straight season, they’ll need to get hot at the right time. They’re warming up as we speak.

item.title: Patriots News: Pats let trade deadline pass, move on to Lions

item.content:encoded:
The Patriots front office let the trade deadline pass without making any moves. There were a number of reasons for this, the best being that the price of the players being offered was too high. Eliot Wolf and crew were right in guarding the team’s draft assets. I get that it’s disappointing to see contenders acquiring players to support their playoff runs. It’s similar to when fans would watch the Pats trade out of the first round at the Draft, watching all the players they’ve become attached to find homes in other cities. But that’s what bad front offices do – make trades just to make a splash, give the impression that they’re dynamic, and then pay the price next year when they’re trying to build a roster with significantly less capital.

These discussions and debates continue to make the NFL world go round.

Plenty of links below to get you ready to dive into Week 10 – or feel like you’re in a barrel heading for the Falls. Enjoy!

item.title: No quarterback in NFL history has done what Bo Nix is doing
item.description: Another week – another fourth quarter comeback and game-winning drive for Bo Nix. He now has 13 and 16 respectively in 43 games started. That’s one 4QC every 3.3 GS and one game-winning drive every 2.7 GS. If you do the rate stats per game started most of the top 10 are names that most […]
item.content:encoded:
Another week – another fourth quarter comeback and game-winning drive for Bo Nix. He now has 13 and 16 respectively in 43 games started. That’s one 4QC every 3.3 GS and one game-winning drive every 2.7 GS.

If you do the rate stats per game started most of the top 10 are names that most NFL fans have forgotten, and this is because QBs with long career generally don’t spend much time playing for a team with a combination of offensive and defensive proficiency/deficiency that leads to many opportunities for them. They are either playing in wins where they get the lead and keep it, or games when they are getting blown out most of the time. Close games were rare (at least until this year). Even some of the greats didn’t have this much opportunity at roughly the same points in their careers.

There were 154 one score games in the 2025 regular season. In the 2006 season there were 132. In the 1996 season there were only 117. We are half-way through the 2026 NFL regular season and there have already been 77 one-score games so they are occurring at the exact same rate as last season. The league loves parity (not to be confused with parody) and that is what they are getting with all of these close games.

The Broncos appear to not be making any moves at running back so let’s talk about the Bronco run game so far. The Broncos are 21st in rushing success rate at 45.8. That is slightly below average. A successful run gains 40 percent of the needed yards on first down, 60 percent on second down, and converts on third or fourth down.

Looking at yards before contact per attempt is one way to see how well the OL of a given team is blocking. Right now RJ Harvey and Jonah Coleman are doing significantly better than JK Dobbins running behind the same offensive line. Coleman is getting 2.6 and Harvey is getting 2.4 while Dobbins is getting 1.7.

Now, I’m sure some of you will think back to how badly Ben Powers and Mike McGlinchey looked run blocking last game and say “It’s the OL not the RB.” But you would be wrong. Those are a few instances and in general the OL has been doing fairly well at run blocking this season. JK Dobbins has just lost a step relative to last season. Coleman and Harvey have also had much better success rates so far this year on runs than Dobbins.

The Bronco defense allowed a conversion on 4th and 18 last game on a play that would have effectively ended the game if the the defense could have stopped the conversion. So far this season the Broncos have been terrible at stopping teams on 3rd (or 4th) and long. They have allowed conversion on 20 of 63 plays.

The Bears have been the best so far and the Ravens have been the worst.

item.title: Are the Washington Commanders still suffering a Week 5 hangover?
item.description: We talk about the Commander in our weekly ‘5 questions’ segment.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants face the Washington Commanders on Thursday, the second and final meeting of the season between the two NFC East teams. We turn to Andrew York of Hogs Haven to answer our ‘5 questions’.

Ed: How have the Commanders moved on from the dysfunctional way that the Week 5 game against the Giants ended? Is there still a hangover from that?

Andrew: It’s funny, because the Giants fumbled away a chance at the win in overtime when they could have made a field goal to win, yet all the media scrutiny seemed to be on the Commanders… However, I’d agree that the decision making around the very last play drew lots of justified criticism on both the Commanders coaching and Jayden Daniels for not having better situational awareness. It was followed up with a similar end-of-game play against the 49ers the very next week that drew criticism of both the coaches and Jayden Daniels. I think that double whammy got people looking at everything a bit more closely, but it’s really just been a litany of questionable decisions (mostly with the coaching and offensive playcalling) over multiple games that has Commanders fans unhappy with their play on the field. Most of the scrutiny has been on OC David Blough, who skipped a few grade levels going from Assistant QB Coach to OC when maybe he needed more time to learn his craft. I honestly put that more on Dan Quinn for promoting him too quickly though, I wouldn’t expect anyone to do well with that big of a promotion.

Ed: Jameis Winston was the Giants’ quarterback in Week 5. Now, it will be J.J. McCarthy. Does that change anything for the Commanders?

Andrew: From a gameplanning standpoint, sure, mainly in that McCarthy is a mobile QB and the defense will have to account for his scrambles. McCarthy also seems to have done a better job throwing deep this year. However, those are just things they’ll have to account for in the gameplan. I don’t think it provides more of a challenge over QBs like Brock Purdy that they’ve already faced. His mobility might be the biggest challenge, as the Commanders allowed Jalen Hurts to scramble for 46 yards earlier this year, getting several critical first downs.

Ed: Can Dan Quinn possibly keep his job if this turns into a four- or five-win season for the Commanders?

Andrew: I don’t think so. The biggest problem for the Commanders seems to be coaching, with the most yards erased by penalty in the NFL, slow playcalls and players taking too much time to get into position, and regular mistakes in situational awareness and game management that lose games. The defense has looked better coached the last few games with the addition of Steve Wilks as a defensive consultant, but it speaks very poorly of Dan Quinn (a supposedly defensive head coach) that he had to bring in an external defensive consultant to improve the defense mid-season. 

Ed: I can’t ask you my “which Giants player would you take for the Commanders” question since we did that a couple of weeks ago. Let me ask this: Which Giants star player do you fear more — Arvell Reese or Malik Nabers?

Andrew: I suppose Arvell Reese simply for the fact that he can directly injure Jayden Daniels on a play, whereas that’s not very likely for Nabers. Keeping Jayden healthy and getting him more experience should be one of the top priorities for a team that is on the outside looking in for any sort of relevance in the postseason.

Ed: NFL teams change constantly. How have the Commanders changed since Week 5, and have those changes made them better or worse?

Andrew: There are two big ways they’ve changed, one negative and one positive. In terms of the negative, they’re more injured. Terry McLaurin suffered a patellar tendon tear and may never be the same player again. DTs Javon Kinlaw and Daron Payne have both gone on IR and are likely done for the year. RB Jacory Croskey-Merritt has gone on IR and won’t be back for a few weeks. That’s $74M in salary cap on injured reserve. 

On the positive side, the defense looks better coached. This largely coincides with the hiring of Steve Wills as a defensive consultant several weeks ago, as mentioned earlier. For some reason, the Commanders didn’t fire or hire any defensive position coaches in the offseason, despite hiring a new defensive coordinator. That means DC Daronte Jones didn’t get to bring staff with him that knew his scheme and instead had to work with the terrible defensive position coaches that coached a historically bad defense last year. Wilks has seemed to help with teaching the defense (and particularly the secondary) their responsibilities, which has resulted in fewer players looking confused and out of place after giving up big plays. The defense looked better coached the last few games, here’s hoping it continues.

item.title: Eagles aren’t rebuilding. They’re retooling, with the immense draft capital as the backbone.
item.description: The Eagles know they can turn this around quickly, with the draft capital as reinforcements to build another contender.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL trade deadline came and went for the Philadelphia Eagles, with the lone move in the days leading up to the deadline being the departure of Jordan Davis.

Surprising? Not really, it’s hard to sell players off in the NFL — even for a team with a 2-7 record.

It’s even harder to negotiate with a general manager like Howie Roseman, a savant at holding onto his players until he can deal them at the right price. See Davis and Cam Jurgens, the other in-season deal the Eagles made prior to the deadline that some seem to (already) forget about.

The Eagles got a 2027 first-round pick, 2027 fifth-round pick, 2028 second-round pick, and 2029 second-round pick for Jurgens and Davis — two players drafted in 2022 that clearly weren’t going to be part of the next era of Eagles football.

Philadelphia also gave up a 2027 seventh-round pick in the Jurgens deal, and almost recouped a higher pick if the Arnold Ebiketie deal didn’t fall through. Add in the 2028 first-round pick and 2027 fifth-round pick in the A.J. Brown deal five months ago and the Eagles are set for the future.

The Eagles have a massive haul of draft picks coming their way over the next three years in the first three rounds — 13 in total.

  • Two first-round picks in 2027 (own and Jaguars), two first-round picks in 2028 (own and Patriots), first-round pick in 2029 (own)
  • Second-round pick in 2027 (own), two second-round picks in 2028 (own and Ravens), two second-round picks in 2029 (own and Jaguars)
  • Third-round pick in 2027 (projected compensatory), third-round pick in 2028 (own), third-round pick in 2029 (own)

That’s a lot of draft capital to work for a team that still has a roster with talented players. Roseman saw the core pieces of the next era of Eagles football, enough where he stocked the cupboard with draft picks for a retool.

Roseman has done this in the past with veteran players with big contracts. He dealt away Kiko Alonso and Byron Maxwell in 2016, Carson Wentz in 2021, along with Brown, Jurgens, and Davis in 2026.

The Eagles general manager has done this before, and Super Bowl appearances have come shortly after.

This isn’t a rebuild for the Eagles. Not even close.

Roseman won’t be using all those picks

Just because the Eagles have 10 draft picks in the first two rounds over the next three seasons (13 in the first three rounds in that span), doesn’t mean Roseman will use them all.

Draft picks are assets to Roseman. He will use that draft capital to be aggressive for either a premium player or to move up in the first round. He certainly has the ammunition to make a bold move.

Look at where the Eagles currently stand in the 2027 draft. Their own pick is currently slated to be in the top-5 (per Tankathon) while the Jaguars’ pick is currently 25th. That 25th pick certainly has value to move up in the top-5 and get one of the special players in this draft.

The Eagles could walk away from the first round of the 2027 draft with Colin Simmons, Jeremiah Smith, or Jordan Seaton. Add one of those players to the star-studded core the Eagles already have and they’ll be in excellent shape for 2027.

Oh, and they’ll still have two first-round picks in 2028 with two second-round picks in 2028 and 2029.

Roseman has a history of being aggressive with draft capital. Look at the 2022 draft when the Eagles had three first-round picks.

The Eagles had their own first-round pick, the first-round pick from the Carson Wentz trade (Colts) and the first-round pick from the swapping of first-round picks from the 2021 draft with the Dolphins. In total, the Eagles had three picks in the teens (No. 15, No. 16 and No. 19).

Roseman swapped picks with the Saints, trading No. 16 and No. 19 to the Saints. The highlight of what the Eagles received in the deal was the Saints’ first-round pick (No. 18), a 2023 first-round pick, and a 2024 second-round pick. The Eagles used that draft capital to get A.J. Brown (No. 18 pick), Jalen Carter (2023 first-round pick), and Cooper DeJean (2024 second-round pick) through other maneuvers from Roseman centered around those picks.

Having a lot of premium draft picks can set the Eagles up for teh future, while also winning games in the present.

The Eagles still have a core of good players

The 2-7 record is what it is, and a lot of the Eagles’ stars have not played up to their potential. With that being said, why can’t the core of star players have bounce-back seasons in 2027?

The Eagles still have a core in place of Jalen Hurts, Jalen Carter, Quinyon Mitchell, DeVonta Smith, Jordan Mailata, Saquon Barkley, Cooper DeJean, Jonathan Greenard, and Zack Baun. They also have good players in Nolan Smith, Moro Ojomo, Jalyx Hunt, and Dontayvion Wicks to build around.

Add in another premier player in the 2027 draft (or two) and develop young players like Jihaad Campbell and Makai Lemon — things can turn around quickly. Who knows? Maybe Markel Bell, Eli Stowers, and Andrew Mukuba improve too.

Hunt isn’t going to have a year like this one in 2027, and neither will Greenard if he’s healthy. The same goes for DeJean.

Also important to remember the Eagles offense is currently on their QB5 (Joe Milton), RB7 (Elijah Mitchell), a very limited Barkley, their WR3 (Lemon), WR4 (Darius Cooper), and WR5 (Hollywood Brown) heading into the bye week. That cast won’t be the offense in 2027.

Even with likely coaching changes across the board, the Eagles still have a core in place to win in 2027 and 2028. There’s uncertainty at a few positions (mainly Hurts’ health and the offensive line), but the talent is there for a quick turnaround.

History is on Roseman’s side

Since Roseman retook the Executive Vice President of Football Operations role from Chip Kelly in 2015, the Eagles have made quick turnarounds from seasons that signaled a lengthy rebuild.

Rebuilds never happen with the Eagles, just retooling of the roster.

The Eagles finished 7-9 in 2015. Roseman took over at the end of that season, hired Doug Pederson in 2016 and went 7-9 with a makeshift roster. Thanks to a strong offseason, the Eagles went 13-3 and won their first Super Bowl title just two seasons after that 7-9 campaign in 2015.

The Eagles went 4-11-1 in 2020, and Roseman traded franchise quarterback Carson Wentz and gave the reigns to Jalen Hurts. He also fired Doug Pederson and hired Nick Sirianni in that same offseason. Philadelphia went 9-8 and make the playoffs in 2021, then went 14-3 to win the NFC Championship in 2022 and made Super Bowl LVII.

Philadelphia won the Super Bowl two years later.

Even before Roseman, the Eagles have had quick turnarounds. Here’s how the Eagles responded from every losing season this century.

  • 1999: 5-11 (11-5 in 2000, made playoffs)
  • 2005: 6-10 (10-6 in 2006, won NFC East)
  • 2012: 4-11-1 (10-6 in 2013, won NFC East)
  • 2015: 7-9 (7-9 in 2016, missed playoffs)
  • 2016: 7-9 (13-3 in 2017, won Super Bowl)
  • 2020: 4-11-1 (9-8 in 2021, made playoffs)

The Eagles have the structure in place to make a quick turnaround again. This is why they didn’t sell off more players at the deadline.

The front office and power structure are in place to turn the franchise around quickly. Even with a few subpar drafts by Roseman that lacked instant impact players, it’s hard to ignore the impact of the 2021-2024 draft classes and how vital they were to the greatest era of football in Eagles history.

Roseman has earned the benefit of the doubt. He’s done this before on multiple occasions.

Why can’t he do it again? Especially with more draft capital and a talented core already in place.

item.title: NFL Panic Meter: While other NFC contenders loaded up at deadline, Rams and Lions were quiet
item.description: The trade deadline was active, but not in Los Angeles or Detroit.
item.content:encoded:
The theme of the trade deadline seemed to be contenders being more aggressive than ever before in their pursuit of a Super Bowl, particularly in the NFC.

That's what made the inactivity of the Detroit Lions and Los Angeles Rams a bit startling.

The Seattle Seahawks, Chicago Bears and San Francisco 49ers all made trades to help themselves now. The Green Bay Packers did not, but they're getting Micah Parsons back soon and they're relying on that being a big midseason addition. The 49ers did the least of that group, but they're also having the best season in the conference and starting to get a little healthier. And we don't need to count anyone in the NFC East or NFC South as a contender.

The only move the Rams or Lions made was Detroit trading a sixth-round pick to the Jets for safety Andre Cisco, who was a part-time starter for a bad New York team.

Let's start with the Rams, because they had the biggest need and their inactivity goes against their normal mode. The Rams have lost Puka Nacua and Davante Adams to injuries, and don't know if they'll be back before it's too late. They're dreadfully thin at receiver for the next few weeks, at least. The Rams have gone from preseason Super Bowl favorite to probably a slight underdog to even make the playoffs. Yet, they did not make a trade before the deadline. The Rams could argue, like the Packers, that adding Myles Garrett back is their in-season addition. But that doesn't help at receiver, and it's hard to believe the Rams have championship upside building a passing game around three or four tight ends and nothing else. It seems like the Rams put three-quarters of their chips in the middle, then folded.

The Lions probably could have used a cornerback or linebacker nearly as much as the Rams needed a receiver, but they did nothing other than a low-cost move to add Cisco. Detroit's defense probably isn't good enough to win a championship, and their fans will be frustrated after seeing other teams, particularly in the NFC North, make moves. They were clamoring for a cornerback for weeks and Jack Campbell's injury left them with a weakness at linebacker. Those areas of need still exist.

The Rams have a "forget them picks" attitude but it still has a limit. They gave up a lot to get Garrett and Trent McDuffie in the offseason. They might have also privately seen a team that is slipping further from being a Super Bowl contender and didn't want to chase their losses. The Lions didn't want to pay the escalating prices to make a huge move on the back end of their defense, and while that might be prudent for the long haul, Detroit fans don't want to be patient anymore. Maybe the Lions or Rams still make a deep playoff run, but they'll have to do it against teams that got much better over the past couple weeks.

Panic meter: The Rams and Lions are still good, but everyone around them got better.

Is now the right time for Fernando Mendoza?

The biggest secondary domino from the trade deadline moves happened with the Las Vegas Raiders. Trading Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings kicked off the Mendoza era. The No. 1 overall pick will be the team's starter going forward.

The timing isn't perfect. The next two games for the Raiders are against the Seahawks and Broncos, two of the toughest defenses in the NFL. The Broncos game is at Denver, which is a tough place to play.

It could be rough for Mendoza early on. The Raiders had to make the move when the Vikings offered a third-round pick for a 38-year-old quarterback who was probably starting only two more games for them anyway. Two games won't ruin the rookie but he's in for a welcome to the NFL moment or two.

Panic meter: Mendoza will be fine but expect some early struggles.

Patriots are thin at RB

Rhamondre Stevenson has an injured tendon in his knee, TreVeyon Henderson has been out with a murky injury and that led people to believe the Patriots could trade for a running back. That didn't happen.

No running backs moved at the trade deadline. The Colts were reportedly asking way too much in return for Jonathan Taylor (more on Indianapolis in a moment) and perhaps the prices of others like Tony Pollard were egregious too. But now the Patriots move forward for a while with Corey Kiner as the lead back. That will put more pressure on Drake Maye, who is coming off a poor game against the Packers. The dream of contending in the AFC East is slipping away. Will the Patriots be a playoff team?

Panic meter: The Patriots should still sneak in the playoffs, but a running back trade would have been nice.

What were the Colts doing?

The Colts traded an eight-time Pro Bowl guard, a three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle. a six-time Pro Bowl receiver and a 25-year-old receiver who has shown promise, and somehow they didn't get a first- or second-round pick back for any of them.

The Colts got a lot of mid-round picks back for Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, but they didn't seem to maximize the value of any of them other than perhaps Allen. Buckner's return of a fourth-round pick seemed quite light given what some other defensive tackles went for. And the Jonathan Taylor situation was just odd.

The Colts reportedly received offers of a second-round pick and more for Taylor and passed. Taylor is a great player but he's a running back on a team with a long rebuild ahead of it. It made little sense to hold on to him. But the Colts, who don't have next year's first-round pick due to the Sauce Gardner trade, don't have much of a plan.

Panic meter: The Colts have a long rebuild ahead and this isn't a good sign it'll go well.

Did the Bengals do enough?

The Bengals can argue that trading the 10th overall pick of the draft for defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II in the offseason was their big move. But some more might have been nice.

The Bengals are getting an MVP-level season from quarterback Joe Burrow, their offensive line is better than it has been in years and the defense has been competent. That defense could be better, though. Couldn't they have outbid the Broncos for Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley, who went for fourth- and fifth-round picks?

The Bengals' ownership has always been ripped for being cheap and maybe that was part of the team making no moves before the deadline. Either way, it's a team that should have Super Bowl hopes and might regret not doing anything to improve itself with another trade.

Panic meter: The Bengals are good but might ultimately find they're a piece or two away.

Nine weeks into the NFL season, we've seen enough from this rookie class to know who's for real, who's still finding their footing and who could make some noise down the stretch. From Carnell Tate's impressive start in Tennessee to Fernando Mendoza getting his opportunity in Las Vegas, here's my midseason check-in on 15 rookies, and what I'm expecting for the rest of the season.

Most Valuable Rookies Rest of Season

Carnell Tate, WR, Tennessee Titans

Carnell Tate has been everything we hoped he would be — and then some. Through seven games, he's hauled in 34 receptions for 413 yards and a touchdown despite playing in one of the more inconsistent passing offenses in football. Cam Ward and the Tennessee Titans haven't exactly made life easy for their rookie receiver, but Tate continues to produce.

The talent is undeniable, the opportunity is there and the chemistry with Ward continues to develop. I expect Tate to build on what's already been a successful rookie campaign. He's a weekly fantasy starter with plenty of room to grow.

Jonah Coleman, RB, Denver Broncos

Jonah Coleman might be the rookie running back I'm most excited about for the second half of the season. He's rushed for 191 yards and three touchdowns while adding 13 receptions for another 128 yards. More importantly, look at how Denver is using him. He handled 21 touches in Week 9, and the coaching staff clearly trusts him.

With R.J. Harvey on injured reserve and J.K. Dobbins getting older, the opportunity is sitting right in front of Coleman. He's already shown he can contribute in the passing game and handle meaningful carries. I wouldn't be surprised if Coleman finishes as one of the most valuable rookie running backs in fantasy.

Omar Cooper Jr., WR, New York Jets

Omar Cooper Jr. missed time early in the season, but the moment he got healthy, he made his presence felt. Through four games, Cooper has 20 receptions for 306 yards and two touchdowns, including back-to-back 100-yard performances. In Week 9, he followed those outings with eight receptions for 58 yards while Garrett Wilson was sidelined.

What I've really liked is the rapport he's developing with Geno Smith. Cooper looks comfortable; he's earning opportunities and he's showing he can win in different areas of the field. Wilson's return could impact his volume, but I'm buying what we've seen. Cooper has legitimate weekly flex appeal moving forward.

KC Concepcion Jr. / Denzel Boston, WRs, Cleveland Browns

KC Concepcion Jr. has quietly been one of the most impressive rookie wide receivers in football. He's sitting at 37 receptions for 437 yards and a touchdown, including 251 receiving yards over his last three games. What jumps off the screen is his ability to create after the catch. Get this young man the football in space and let him work.

The Browns haven't exactly provided consistent quarterback play, but Concepcion continues to find ways to produce. He's dynamic, explosive and already showing flashes of a player who could eventually become a Pro Bowl-caliber receiver. For fantasy purposes, he's worked his way into weekly flex consideration.

And how about Denzel Boston? The rookie has 507 receiving yards and three touchdowns on 32 receptions. Boston gives me some young Mike Evans vibes with his size, downfield ability and willingness to go make contested catches. He's already producing explosive plays despite the limitations of this Browns offense.

What's encouraging is that both Boston and Concepcion are earning significant opportunities without cannibalizing each other's production. Boston has legitimate big-play upside every single week and continues to look like one of the steals of the rookie class. I love what we've seen and expect a strong finish.

Germie Bernard, WR, Pittsburgh Steelers

Germie Bernard's rookie season has been a little up and down, but I've seen enough to remain encouraged. He's caught 32 passes for 284 yards and a touchdown, highlighted by a phenomenal 11-reception performance in Week 6. The following two games weren't nearly as productive, but I wouldn't let that discourage you.

Bernard has established himself as a trusted option for Aaron Rodgers in a Pittsburgh offense that's been better than advertised. His role makes sense. Get him the football quickly, let him operate in space and allow his natural ability to take over. Bernard feels like a buy-low candidate with a solid second-half outlook.

Fernando Mendoza, QB, Las Vegas Raiders

I can't believe I'm putting Fernando Mendoza on this list, but here we are. The No. 1 overall pick is taking over as the Raiders' starting quarterback after Kirk Cousins was traded to Minnesota. Mendoza has attempted just eight regular-season passes, completing six for 48 yards, so we have almost nothing to evaluate.

But here's what we do know: Cousins threw 20 touchdowns in nine games and Mendoza gets to operate in that same Klint Kubiak offense featuring Brock Bowers. Listen, any quarterback throwing to Brock Bowers gets a touchdown bonus in my book. Add Ashton Jeanty, Trey Tucker and a potentially more favorable schedule down the stretch, and there's legitimate streaming appeal here. I'm not expecting Mendoza to be a league winner, but don't be surprised if he becomes fantasy relevant sooner than people think.

Still Need More Information

Jadarian Price, RB, Seattle Seahawks

Jadarian Price is one of those players where the box score doesn't tell the entire story. He's rushed for 172 yards and added 83 receiving yards on 10 catches without scoring a touchdown. The production hasn't been there consistently, but every time he touches the football, you see the explosiveness. Unfortunately, injuries and ball-security issues have limited his opportunities.

With Zach Charbonnet still working his way back from a knee injury, there's a path for Price to earn a larger role. Seattle's offensive line should also improve as it gets healthier. I'm cautiously optimistic, but I need to see him string together consistent performances before trusting him in fantasy lineups.

Makai Lemon, WR, Philadelphia Eagles

Makai Lemon has been better than his rookie numbers might suggest. Through nine games, he's caught 37 passes for 312 yards and one touchdown, including 19 receptions for 185 yards over his last three games. The Eagles offense has been difficult to watch at times, and Lemon has dealt with inconsistent quarterback play while occasionally being asked to operate as the team's top receiver with DeVonta Smith unavailable.

What I've loved is his ability to separate, particularly against zone coverage. He's consistently finding openings and earning targets. The big fantasy performances haven't arrived yet, but the underlying usage is encouraging. There's more here than the box score suggests.

Jordyn Tyson, WR, New Orleans Saints

We finally got our first look at Jordyn Tyson, and while it wasn't perfect, there were encouraging signs. In his NFL debut, Tyson caught four passes for 30 yards but also lost a fumble on his first reception. I'm not worried about that. What matters is that New Orleans immediately looked to get him involved.

This Saints offense ranks among the league leaders in neutral-situation pass rate, meaning the opportunity should continue to be there. Getting Calvin Banks back should help Tyler Shough operate more comfortably behind that offensive line. The biggest question remains Tyson's health. If that hamstring holds up, I'm expecting his role to expand significantly.

Mike Washington Jr., RB, Las Vegas Raiders

Mike Washington Jr. gave us one of the more surprising rookie performances of the season when he handled 25 carries for 83 yards. Then he turned around the following week and rushed six times for -3 yards. That's been the problem. Washington has 275 rushing yards and a touchdown this season, but his role remains difficult to project.

Neither Washington nor Ashton Jeanty has consistently found success running behind this Raiders offensive line. Washington clearly has some ability, but can this coaching staff establish a defined role for him? Until that happens, he's difficult to trust. He's an interesting stash with upside if Jeanty misses time.

Biggest Disappointment

Jeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals

There's no bigger fantasy disappointment from this rookie class than Jeremiyah Love. And before anybody gets upset, I'm not putting all of that on the player. Love has rushed for 268 yards, added just 36 receiving yards and scored two total touchdowns in six games. We've seen flashes of the talent that made him such a highly regarded prospect, but the situation in Arizona has been a disaster.

The offense has struggled, the quarterback situation has deteriorated and now Love is sitting on injured reserve. If you invested a second-, third- or fourth-round fantasy pick in him, there's no way around it — it's been disappointing. The talent hasn't disappeared, but the fantasy return simply hasn't been there.

Could Matter More Down the Stretch

Antonio Williams, WR, Washington Commanders

Antonio Williams is one of those rookies who could become much more relevant over the second half of the season. He's caught 26 passes for 284 yards and a touchdown, including eight receptions for 79 yards over his last two games. The problem hasn't necessarily been Williams. It's been the Commanders’ offense.

Jayden Daniels continues to deal with a significant elbow injury and Washington hasn't been particularly creative offensively. We've also seen Williams have some unfortunate plays wiped away. With Terry McLaurin out, there should be additional opportunities available. He's not a weekly fantasy starter yet, but there's a path for Williams to become a useful flex option.

Emmett Johnson, RB, Kansas City Chiefs

Emmett Johnson has quietly put together 348 yards from scrimmage and two total touchdowns, including that ridiculous 128-yard receiving performance against Denver in Week 8. We saw a 73-yard touchdown reception and a player who can absolutely make things happen with the football in his hands.

The problem? Kenneth Walker III has been phenomenal since arriving in Kansas City.

Johnson isn't taking that starting job anytime soon. But what if the Chiefs can turn him into a Jerick McKinnon-type receiving weapon? There's potential for standalone fantasy value in that role. And if Walker were to miss time, Johnson immediately becomes one of the most valuable backups in football.

Kaelon Black, RB, San Francisco 49ers

Kaelon Black has 303 rushing yards and a touchdown this season, and I don't think enough people are paying attention to what he's doing. That's more rushing production than Jeremiyah Love, Mike Washington Jr. and Jadarian Price. The biggest obstacle is obvious: Christian McCaffrey.

But we've seen San Francisco utilize multiple backs at times, and keeping McCaffrey fresh has to remain a priority. Black has demonstrated that he can be an effective runner when given opportunities. The receiving game hasn't been a major part of his role, so there are limitations to his standalone fantasy value. Still, this is a player I want rostered heading into the second half of the season.
