item.title: Cat Scratch Reader Reacts Week 9: Confidence and outrage
item.description: I think the NFL got it wrong. What about you?
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers lost another close game in which their lack of top end talent, thanks primarily to injuries, proved the difference. It is hard to evaluate much about this team when so many of their starters are missing, but such is our duty as fans: to judge failure as harshly as we celebrate success.

Then, of course, there is the elephant-sized zebra in the room. The Panthers had the ball stripped from them on the goal line by the officials and handed to the Broncos over a challenge that Sean Payton threw as the ball was being snapped on the next play. Officials let the play continue because they did not see the flag and then announced there was a flag.

Multiple video angles from fans in the stands show Payton throwing the flag up to 0.1 seconds before the snap on second and goal, with the flag landing on the ground well after the play commenced.

There are two pieces of language that are relevant here. The first is the NFL rule book:

The head coach or head coach’s pregame challenge designee can initiate a challenge by throwing a red flag onto the field of play before the next legal snap or kick.

The next is the postgame comment from the referee:

Replay can get involved to make sure that the head coach throws his challenge flag prior to the next snap,” Butterworth said. “We were actually able to use angles to show that the flag was out prior to the ball being snapped, and so we permitted the challenge.

There seems to be some discrepancy between “the flag was out” and “onto the field of play” to me. What do you think?

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Panthers fans and fans across the country.

Did the officials get it right?

Are you confident in the Panthers?

item.title: Bears v. Buccaneers Upon Further Review: A Closer Look at the Referees
item.description: Check out @GOOCH1701's weekly look at the official's calls and the no-calls from the Bears vs. Buccaneers game.
item.content:encoded:
Upon Further Review — Week 9: Bears 27, Buccaneers 24
Sunday Night, November 8, 2026. Soldier Field, Chicago.
Crew: Ronald Torbert (R #62), Barry Anderson (U #20), Jay Bilbo (DJ #84), Tripp Sutter (LJ #37), Ryan Dickson (FJ #25), Keith Washington (SJ #7), Courtney Brown (BJ #48), Kevin Stine (RO #0).

Hello Chicago Bears fans! Well, what to say about this one? Chicago survived a turnover-filled night at Soldier Field and left with a 27–24 walk-off win on Cairo Santos’s 38-yard field goal. So how did the officating affect this game? Spoiler alert: quite a bit. Official totals: Bears 9–74, Buccaneers 8–45. Seventeen total accepted penalties for 119 yards (18 total flags). Every accepted flag and every meaningful no-call is accounted for in our review. Let’s get into it.

UFR method: Every accepted flag and every meaningful no-call is graded on the same four-tier scale: Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, Horrible. Weight runs 1–4 by impact: 1 for housekeeping/pre-snap process, 2 for drive disruption or field-position damage, 3 for scoring/red-zone leverage or automatic first down that changes a drive, 4 for wiped score, turnover, or game-ending leverage. Replay overturns are judged against the “clear and obvious” standard. No-calls receive identical grades and weights as thrown flags. Bright-line process fouls (false starts, clear offside, delay of game when the clock hits zero, kickoff short of landing zone) are Correct when the rule is met. Judgment calls (holding, PI, unnecessary roughness) are evaluated against the rule text, available angles, All-22 when reviewed, and broadcast rules analysis. The Flag of the Game is the single most egregious or impactful snap. The League File covers the week’s most contested NFL controversy. And this week we have a special College Flag Focus included for that unbelievable game between Texas and Missouri.

First Quarter

Bears open with a long drive. Rome Odunze 9-yard touchdown from Caleb Williams. Santos kick. CHI 7, TB 0. Luther Burden III then takes a 56-yard touchdown pass from Williams. CHI 14, TB 0.

Kickoff Short of Landing Zone — Cairo Santos (CHI), 0 yards. Q1 9:38.
Santos kicks 42 yards short of the landing zone. Ball placed at the Bucs 40. Bright-line special-teams process. Correct. Wt 1. Cairo is a quality field goal kicker, but he is boom and bust on kickoffs. We may need to consider going another direction if he continues to have these problems.

Second Quarter

Santos and Chase McLaughlin trade field goals. CHI 17, TB 6 at the half.

Delay of Game — Unnamed (TB), 5 yards. Q2 14:07, 4th-and-4 at CHI 4.
Clock expires before the snap on fourth-and-goal. No play. McLaughlin later kicks a 27-yard field goal. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Unnecessary Roughness — Zavion Thomas (CHI), 15 yards. Q2 8:37, 1st-and-8 at TB 8.
After D’Andre Swift’s 2-yard run to the TB 6, Thomas is flagged for late contact to the helmet on a block. Enforced at the TB 6. Backs the Bears up and contributes to a later interception. Bright-line late hit. Correct. Wt 2.

False Start — Tristan Wirfs (TB), 5 yards. Q2 5:35, 3rd-and-5.
Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

False Start — Cade Otton (TB), 5 yards. Q2 2:56, 1st-and-10.
Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

False Start — Cody Mauch (TB), 5 yards. Q2 0:25, 2nd-and-10.
Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Defensive Holding — J. Johnson (CHI), 5 yards. Q2 0:25, 2nd-and-15.
Defensive holding flag on Johnson. Available tape and the user’s All-22 review show the contact does not meet the standard for defensive holding. Incorrect. Wt 2.

Third Quarter

Bucky Irving scores from 2 yards. CHI 17, TB 13.

Offensive Holding — D’Marco Jackson (CHI), 10 yards. Q3 11:37 (Flag of the Game).
Zavion Thomas fields the kickoff at the Chicago 8 and returns it 91 yards to the Tampa Bay 1 (pushed out of bounds). Officials flag Jackson for holding. The 10-yard penalty is enforced from the Chicago 30, leaving the Bears at their own 20. Available angles and slow-motion replays show an open-palm block on the chest/shoulder area with no sustained grab of the jersey or restriction that meets the holding standard. Josh Blackwell called it a “terrible call” that “took a touchdown off the board for nothing that was really even there.” Broadcast rules analysis did not support a hold. This is not borderline. Horrible. Wt 4. Erased a near-touchdown or first-and-goal at the 1. We will get into this more with our Flag of the Game highlight.

False Start — Luke Goedeke (TB), 5 yards. Q3 10:31, 1st-and-10.
Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Offensive Holding — Stephen Carlson (CHI), 9 yards. Q3 7:26, 3rd-and-1.
Holding flag on Carlson. Judgment call on technique. Available angles show borderline restriction. Arguable. Wt 2.

Offensive Holding — Bauer Sharp (TB), 10 yards. Q3 6:52, 1st-and-10.
Holding flag on Sharp. Judgment call. Arguable. Wt 2.

False Start — Jack Sanborn (CHI), 5 yards. Q3 0:33, 4th-and-4.
Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Jaylon Johnson intercepts Baker Mayfield and returns it 67 yards for a touchdown. CHI 24, TB 13.

Fourth Quarter

McLaughlin field goal. CHI 24, TB 16.

Delay of Game — Unnamed (TB), 5 yards. Q4 11:28, 4th-and-4.
Clock expires. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Delay of Game — Unnamed (CHI), 5 yards. Q4 8:10, 4th-and-7.
Clock expires. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

False Start — Tristan Wirfs (TB), 5 yards. Q4 7:25, 2nd-and-3.
Pre-snap movement. Bright-line. Correct. Wt 1.

Face Mask — Austin Booker (CHI), 15 yards. Q4 7:19, 3rd-and-8.
Booker is flagged for grabbing the facemask while sacking Mayfield. Clear contact. Correct. Wt 2.

Offensive Holding — Cam Lewis (CHI), 10 yards. Q4 4:41, 4th-and-11.
Holding flag on Lewis. Judgment call on special teams or coverage technique. Arguable. Wt 2.

Unnecessary Roughness — Anthony Robinson (TB), declined. Q4 0:03.
Flagged on the final play sequence; declined. Bright-line if enforced. Correct (declined). Wt 1.

No-call: Helmet-to-helmet hit on Luther Burden III by Rueben Bain Jr. (fumble + concussion).
Late fourth quarter, third-and-long near the Bears’ own 15–17. Williams throws a short screen to Burden. Bain delivers clear helmet-to-helmet contact. Burden’s head is driven into the turf; he is knocked unconscious, fumbles, and is diagnosed with a concussion (confirmed by Ben Johnson postgame). Ifeatu Melifonwu recovers. No flag. The contact is forcible to the head/neck area on a player who had just caught the ball and was still a receiver. It is not incidental shoulder-to-chest. The play produces a turnover that Tampa Bay converts into a touchdown and two-point conversion to tie the game at 24. Incorrect (no-call). Wt 4. Had the flag been thrown, the fumble is wiped, Chicago keeps the ball with a 15-yard penalty and automatic first down, and the tying score does not happen on that possession.

Bears answer with a drive featuring a 38-yard pass to Colston Loveland. Santos hits the 38-yard walk-off field goal. CHI 27, TB 24 final.

Calls and No-Calls Against Chicago (every accepted flag + covered no-calls, individual lines)

Chicago accepted: 9–74. Every accepted flag listed individually above, plus the covered no-call.

Calls and No-Calls Against Tampa Bay (every accepted flag + covered no-calls, individual lines)

Tampa Bay accepted: 8–45. Every accepted flag listed individually above.

Crew card (Ronald Torbert): Accepted flags mostly Correct on bright-line process fouls (false starts, delays of game, kickoff short, face mask, unnecessary roughness on Thomas). One Horrible against Chicago (Jackson holding that wiped the Thomas return). One Incorrect against Chicago (defensive holding on Johnson). One Incorrect no-call against the Bucs (Bain helmet-to-helmet on Burden that produced the fumble and concussion). No Horrible flags against Tampa Bay.

Differential. Accepted volume is close (9–74 vs. 8–45), but the two Weight-4 items both hurt Chicago: the Horrible holding call that erased a near-touchdown return, and the Incorrect no-call on the Burden hit that flipped possession and produced the tying score. Those two snaps represent the largest officiating swing of the night. The game was ultimately decided by the Bears’ defense (Jaylon Johnson pick-six) and Santos’s walk-off kick more than by the cumulative process flags.

Grade: One Horrible and one Incorrect against Chicago; one Incorrect no-call against Tampa Bay. Otherwise clean enough on the process tape.

Flag of the Game: Offensive holding on D’Marco Jackson, third quarter.

Early in the third quarter, Tampa Bay had just cut the lead to 17–13 on Bucky Irving’s 2-yard touchdown. On the ensuing kickoff, Zavion Thomas fielded the ball at the Chicago 8 and raced 91 yards down the left sideline to the Tampa Bay 1, where he was pushed out of bounds. Tracking data later showed Thomas reached 21.8 mph (fourth-fastest ball-carrier speed of the season) and covered 111.5 yards of total distance on the return. It was the closest he has come to a return touchdown this year.

Officials flagged linebacker D’Marco Jackson for offensive holding. The 10-yard penalty was enforced from the Chicago 30, leaving the Bears at their own 20 — a net loss of roughly 79 yards of field position. Chicago gained seven yards on the next three plays and punted. The near-score was erased.

Available angles and slow-motion replays show Jackson delivering an open-palm block into the chest/shoulder area of a Buccaneers defender. There is no sustained grab of the jersey, no wrapping of the arm, and no clear restriction that meets the standard for offensive holding on a special-teams return. Broadcast rules analysis did not support the call. The contact is the kind of physical engagement that occurs on nearly every kickoff return block.

Player reaction (Josh Blackwell, postgame):
“Terrible call. I didn’t think it was a good call. You just took a touchdown off the board for nothing that was really even there. That’s annoying.”

Fan and media reaction (selected):

  • “That’s really bad.”
  • “Horrible call.”
  • “That wasn’t even holding.”
  • “Bulls—t call!”
  • “AWFUL CALL.”
  • “Fake a-s penalty.”
  • “Soft f——-g call.”
  • “A flag negates a beautiful 92-yard kickoff return by Zavion Thomas. That was NOT a penalty.”
  • “Zero accountability, zero repercussions, same [expletive] every week.”
  • Chicago Sun-Times: “A D’Marco Jackson hold — questionable, but a hold — brought back a 91-yard kickoff return by Zavion Thomas.”
  • One write-up called it a “phantom penalty.”

Jackson’s flag alone shifted Chicago’s starting position by approximately 79 yards. The Bears went from first-and-goal at the 1 (or a near-touchdown) to needing 80 yards. In a game that finished 27–24, the swing was massive. Replay cannot review the judgment of whether holding occurred; only the administration of the penalty is reviewable. The call stands as one of the clearest examples this season of a non-existent hold wiping a game-changing special-teams play.

UFR grade remains Horrible, Weight 4. It is not borderline. It is not a close judgment call. It is an egregiously wrong flag that removed a near-touchdown and handed the Buccaneers a massive field-position advantage in a one-score game.

League File — Broncos vs. Panthers, Nov. 8.
Devon Key end-zone interception after Sean Payton challenge-flag timing.

Bryce Young’s pass to Tommy Tremble in the end zone is tipped and intercepted by Broncos safety Devon Key before the ball hits the ground. Officials rule incomplete. Carolina lines up and snaps the next play (Chuba Hubbard stuffed at the 1). After the play ends, officials announce a challenge was granted.

NFL vice president of instant replay Mark Butterworth told the pool reporter that replay angles confirmed Payton’s red challenge flag was out prior to the snap, so the challenge was permitted. The review overturned the call to an interception (touchback). Denver took over, drove for a touchdown, and won 26–21.

The interception itself is clear on the tape. The process controversy is whether the flag was timely. Officials used additional angles to confirm it was out before the snap. On broadcast and some sideline views it looked extremely close or after. Under the rule as applied by the replay center, the challenge was allowed. The sequence is unusual: a full play was run before the challenge was processed. Weight 4 (turnover that flipped a potential score into a touchback and subsequent Denver score).

College Flag Focus — Texas vs. Missouri (Nov. 7, 2026). No. 7 Texas 34, No. 18 Missouri 20.

Focus play: Arch Manning “fumble” ruled incomplete forward pass.
Third-and-10, Missouri leading 20–13 late in the third. Manning is hit by Brian Huff as he begins his throwing motion. The ball comes out forward, travels ~14 yards downfield, and is recovered by Texas. Officials rule fumble on the field. Replay upholds. Texas keeps the ball and scores a touchdown three plays later to tie the game, then scores 21 unanswered.

The ball leaves Manning’s hand with clear forward movement as part of a pass attempt. There is no immediate recovery by Texas; the ball is loose and travels downfield before a Texas player gathers it. Rules analysis (Steve Shaw on the broadcast) noted that any intentional forward movement of the hand with control makes it an incomplete pass. Commenttors Joe Tessitore and Jesse Palmer ciriticized the call. The ruling on the field and the upheld review treat it as a fumble. This is Incorrect (and borderline Horrible given the impact). Weight 4. It wiped a likely punt and produced a tying touchdown.

Additional reviews that all went against Missouri:

  • Missed intentional grounding on Manning (no flag).
  • Overturn of a caught pass by replay against Missouri.
  • Receiver with a toe down, ball ruled no catch.
  • Rushing touchdown where the ball appears to break the plane over the pylon; too close for a clear-and-obvious overturn, yet ruled short or incomplete.

Five or more reviews went against the Tigers. The Manning fumble is the clearest and most consequential. The University of Missouri Athletic Director has requested a formal review.

But what did you think about the officiating, in the college games, in the NFL, and in the Bears v. Buccaneers game this week? Tell us in the comments below!

item.title: Cowboys rookie report: One player rises above the rest
item.description: Caleb Downs was awesome last week
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys needed somebody to finish the job, and Caleb Downs answered. After the offense reclaimed the lead late in Indianapolis, the rookie intercepted Daniel Jones to seal a 27–23 victory. His first NFL interception capped an afternoon that also included a sack and gave the Cowboys a much-needed response to last week’s collapse.

But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. 

Caleb Downs

(64 defensive snaps | 3 tackles | 1 TFL | 1 sack | 1 INT | 2 passes defended | 1 QB hit | 1 pressure)

This was the playmaking performance Dallas wanted from its first-round safety. Downs hit Daniel Jones for a blind-side sack, then ended the Colts’ final possession with an interception. His coverage was strong throughout, allowing one completion for 12 yards on four targets.

There was little to criticize in his individual production as he affected the quarterback, limited completions and made the decisive play. That is a strong response after leaving the Arizona game with a concussion. 

Jaishawn Barham

(3 defensive snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits)

Even with DeMarvion Overshown unavailable, Barham barely featured on defense. Shemar James and Dee Winters handled the bulk of the linebacker work. Three snaps offer little room for a fair performance judgement, but the lack of opportunity is the story. He finished without a defensive statistic. His fall has been rapid.

Drew Shelton

(0 offensive snaps | 6 special team snaps)

Shelton was active, but he recorded no offensive snaps. There is no blocking performance to assess and he stayed on the bench other than to come on for special team duties. 

LT Overton

(17 defensive snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits | 1 pressure)

Overton generated one hurry on 10 pass-rush snaps, but otherwise had a quiet afternoon. He did not record a tackle or sack. There was a small contribution to the rush, although Dallas will want more disruption as his opportunities continue. 

Camden Brown

(28 offensive snaps | 0 targets | 0 receptions | 0 receiving yards | 0 TD | 3 kickoff returns, 78 yards)

Brown contributed most visibly as a returner, averaging 26 yards on three kickoffs. His offensive involvement brought no targets despite George Pickens being unavailable. The return work gave him a useful role, but he has yet to turn his receiving opportunities into production.

item.title: Chiefs waive return specialist Nikko Remigio after midseason trade
item.description: Kansas City cut its starting punt returner after trading for a receiver with return experience.
item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday, the Kansas City Chiefs executed a trade to acquire wide receiver Josh Downs from the Indianapolis Colts. To make room on the 53-man roster, the Chiefs reportedly waived rookie defensive end Jack Pyburn. Matt Derrick of ChiefsDigest.comwas the first to report it, but Pyburn was not the only player cut after the midseason move.

On Wednesday morning, the team also announced that wide receiver and return specialist Nikko Remigio was waived. He has been the Chiefs’ primary returner for three seasons, but he is now on waivers and will likely return to the team’s practice squad by the end of the week if he clears.

The former undrafted free agent out of Fresno State in 2023 went from training-camp darling to starter by the 2024 season. To this day, his most memorable play may be the 41-yard punt return in the first half of the AFC Championship Game against the Buffalo Bills, which set up a touchdown drive and helped clinch a third consecutive trip to the Super Bowl.

In each of his three NFL seasons, Remigio’s punt-return average has dropped. In the 2024 regular season, he averaged 9.5 yards per punt return, but this season his average is 5.6 yards; out of 14 “qualified” punt returners, that is the lowest average in the NFL, according to Pro Football Reference.

Rookie running back Emmett Johnson has emerged as a strong option for kick returns, and rookie wideout Cyrus Allen has repped the returner spot in the preseason and last week, though he fumbled his one shot.

It will be worth seeing if Downs becomes an option for Kansas City on punt returns. This season, Downs has returned only two punts for 20 yards, but he has 32 career punt returns in the NFL and averages 9.8 yards per return.

The release of both Remigio and Pyburn frees up a spot on the 53-man roster ahead of the Week 10 matchup against the Atlanta Falcons.

Editor’s note: Second-year defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott (knee) needs to be activated before November 17th, which is next Tuesday, so he could be the player who fills the vacancy.

item.title: Fantasy Football: 4 bold predictions for the second half of the season
item.description: Chris Allen makes four bold fantasy predictions for the second of the season.
item.content:encoded:
Quick peek behind the curtain: I've mentioned it before, but I go back and forth with the staff here at Yahoo Fantasy about which storylines to prioritize. After one drive, we knew the SNF angle would be Caleb Williams and Rome Odunze. Odunze got the first TD; Williams was on fire. However, the Buccaneers came into the second half with a different plan. Even into the fourth quarter, I was thinking we'd have to scrap the idea.

That's where we are with our rosters, too. Nine weeks in, we've got a pretty good handle on who's been reliable or a bust. Maybe too good of a handle. Because the guys who carried us through October aren't guaranteed to do the same in December. Just ask the Bears.

So, let's draw up some bold adjustments — predictions that look wild today but have a real path if things break right. And yes, as a Bengals fan, my first one might be a little biased.

Joe Burrow challenges Josh Allen for the QB1 spot

For the record, I didn't make this prediction. I realize that sounds exactly like something an admitted Cincy fan who loops Bengals notes into every piece of content would say to redirect blame. But as I watched Joe Burrow on Sunday morning, my confidence in the idea of seeing him play in February grew a little.

Joe Burrow has accounted for EIGHTEEN touchdowns in his last FOUR games.

24/29, 271 PASS YDS, 3 PASS TD, 0 INT, 1 RUSH TD vs Falcons.

Burrow is making a serious push for his first MVP award. https://t.co/gY8dTz9mcppic.twitter.com/aRaLRw52SO

— Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 8, 2026

After a, let's call it, shaky performance against the Titans, Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins were back to reminding people they can be a potent offense in the first half of games, too. Shades of LSU Burrow and Chase were on full display. Through nine weeks of the season, there have been 24 instances of a QB having a passing success rate over 60% in a single game. Burrow has three of them (tied for most). A QB has thrown for 3+ TDs in 55 games this season. Joey B accounts for five (most). But before we (me, really) get too far over our skis, let's address the elephant in the room.

  • Aaron Rodgers, 2016

  • Patrick Mahomes, 2018 and 2022

Over the last 10 seasons, a pocket passer has finished as the QB1 just three times. Honestly, "pocket passer" might be underselling things a bit. Even Rodgers ran for 369 at 33 years old. But what either passer could do with their legs averaged out to be 55.3 points per season. Burrow's already at 25.7 after three rushing TDs. Besides, it's the elite efficiency that got them ahead of the Konami QBs anyway.

  • Passing Success Rate: 55.3% (Burrow), 54.9% (Mahomes '22), 53.8% (Mahomes '18), 49.8% (Rodgers)

  • Passing YPG: 298.3, 308.8, 318.6, 276.8

  • TD Rate: 7.8%, 6.3%, 8.6%, 6.6%

Even with the slow start, Burrow's per-down and per-game metrics fall in line with the guys who led their peers in total fantasy points. And, for the other Bengals faithful out there, two of those seasons resulted in an MVP award to the QB1.

I know we've got two more months of action to go. But with the defense lagging and a favorable schedule, Burrow's case for the QB1 isn't as wild as it sounds. 

Jonah Coleman is a top-16 RB in total PPR points

Notice I said "total PPR points" and not points per game. Because that puts Jonah Coleman (well, me, really) at a bit of a disadvantage since the rest of the league has a four-week head start on him. But I'm not too worried.

Is it great to have an explosive running back? Absolutely.

If you don't have an explosive running back, is it nice to have a sustainer who will get six when it's blocked for three, can catch the ball, and adds pass pro?

Here's Jonah Coleman. @Broncospic.twitter.com/g20gYNNb7I

— Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) November 10, 2026

Doug Farrar summed up Coleman perfectly. While the rookie has only two runs to gain more than 10 yards since rejoining the team, you can pull up the film and see why he's played more than J.K. Dobbins. The numbers tell the same story. 

When it's been just Coleman and Dobbins as the Broncos' RBs, Coleman has more than doubled Dobbins' early-down rushing success rate (42.3% vs. 18.2%). Essentially, he's getting Bo Nix into more manageable passing downs. Accordingly, Denver's third-down conversion rate has been up by 20.6% over the last two weeks. Coleman has also been a weapon as a receiver. Almost half of his catches have turned into first downs, and he's averaging 15.0 YAC per reception. And that's just been the last two games. But even when you look at Coleman from a full-season perspective, he's already on his way to being one of the top backs in the league.

  • Rushing Success Rate: 42.6%, 12th (out of 43 qualifiers – min. 60 touches)

  • Forced Missed Tackle Rate: 19.1%, T-17th 

  • Yards per Route Run: 2.33, 2nd 

As I talked about Sunday, Coleman has already relegated Dobbins to the RB2 spot. And look at the Broncos' schedule after their bye. Four of his seven matchups will be against defenses in the top 12 in yards allowed to opposing RBs. And two of the remaining three are units that give up production to pass-catching backs. With Coleman having the talent and situation of an RB1, he has the best shot to finish like one by the end of the fantasy season.

Both Rams RBs finish as fringe RB1s

All I can think of when trying to imagine HC Sean McVay game plan without his top two receivers is Tony Stark building the Mark I suit in a cave. You'd have to think everything is on the table. But his normal response to losing a receiver isn't as viable an option this time, though. 

  • Nacua+Adams Active: 38.9% (2+TE Snap Rate)

  • Either Out: 53.9% 

The Rams made using multiple TEs cool before it became en vogue. But that was when the personnel was available, before Terrance Ferguson had to go on IR or Colby Parkinson had to deal with injuries to his ribs. However, they do have an extra receiver. He just happens to be in the backfield.

WHAT A CATCH AND RUN FROM BLAKE CORUM!!! pic.twitter.com/hu3RQ9CG8z

— Ethan Shirazi (@Ethanshirazi24) October 13, 2026

Blake Corum is one of three RBs with top-10 marks in YPRR (1.68) and YAC per reception (9.9). Zooming in on the Rams offense only lends more credence to the idea that we should see him on the field more often. Of all the Rams' pass-catchers, Corum's 8.5% first-down-per-route run rate ranks third behind only Nacua and Adams. Plus, if the last few weeks have been any indication, McVay was already moving in this direction. 

  • Week 7: 9% (Corum Route Rate), 5.3 (Stafford aDOT), 79.3% (Completion Rate)

  • Week 8: 19%, 3.2, 68.0%

  • Week 9: 22%, 7.1, 60.5%

The Rams already sit at 13th in target rate to their RBs. Kyren Williams has the second-most balls thrown his way of any rusher. Let's assume McVay boosts how often Matthew Stafford looks for his rushers with a weakened receiving corps. In that scenario, Williams and Corum turn into RB1s to close out the '26 season.

Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion end 2026 inside the top 20

Cleveland has the makings of a fantasy-friendly offense for the next half-decade if everyone stays healthy. Even better for the Browns, their rookie WRs are already creating highlights regardless of who's throwing them the ball.

DENZEL BOSTON MOSSED HIM pic.twitter.com/ZZdzSZtnpj

— NFL (@NFL) November 8, 2026

I can already see Denzel Boston making a similar grab against Cincinnati's defense in Week 13; I won't be surprised in the least. That's mostly because the UW product has been doing something similar all season. On throws of 20+ air yards, Boston has the ninth-most receiving yards 195), tied with Ja'Marr Chase and Rome Odunze. But the production doesn't stop at the catch point. As the clip against the Saints shows above, the Browns' WR1 continues churning out yards on downfield throws at the third-highest clip among receivers. But if Boston isn't beating defenders deep, his teammate is working the intermediate area of the field.

a couple of KC Concepcion catch and runs from the same drive. Twitchy twitchy twitchy. pic.twitter.com/hFxDCDZJJ8

— Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) October 27, 2026

KC Concepcion is the ideal complement to Boston's archetype. At an aDOT of 6.8 air yards on the season, Concepcion has top-20 marks in YPRR and YAC per reception (recepcion?). Over a third of his catches have resulted in a first down or a score. Subsequently, Concepcion has been the more fantasy-relevant Browns receiver over the last month, averaging 14.2 PPR PPG. This makes sense, given Concepcion's higher share of lay-up looks (84% catchable target rate over his last four games). Regardless, the two have delineated roles that allow them both to turn in top-20 performances any week, as they did against the Saints. Our only concern is the quality (and quantity) of what we're getting from whoever is under center.

  • Dropbacks per Game (All Browns' QBs): 35.6, 16th 

  • Completion Percentage Over Expected: -0.59%, 20th  

Even with Deshaun Watson retaking the starting job, his uneven play before missing Week 9 is a concern. But with at least four defenses on their upcoming schedule allowing above-average PPG to WRs, both Boston and Denzel have the runway to finish the season inside the top 20.

item.title: Eagles News: Howie Roseman among biggest winners from the NFL trade deadline
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 11/11/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Howie Roseman did not have a very good offseason. That much is hardly the only reason the 2026 Eagles are pretty bad. But it’s certainly part of the equation. That being said, he still very much deserves benefit of the doubt moving forward. And moves like the Jordan Davis trade are exactly why. He can press the right buttons to get this team turned around. He will do his job to put the Eagles in championship contention.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

The Winners and Losers of the NFL Trade Deadline – The Ringer

Winner: Howie Roseman. Over the years, every time the Eagles have made a move—no matter how insignificant—the “HOWIE SZN!!!” posts on social media most likely appeared in your timeline. Sometimes it’s been warranted. Other times it hasn’t. The Jordan Davis trade falls into the former category. Davis has been a nice player for the Eagles, but he has played only 52 percent of the snaps this season. That’s because he is on the sideline for almost every passing situation. To get a first- and a second-round pick for a run-stopping defensive tackle is a minor miracle in 2026. The Eagles have been horrible this year, but they are now positioned to reload with five(!) first-round picks and five(!!) second-round picks in the next three drafts. Roseman’s greatest strength might be realizing when his roster is a mess and figuring out how to escape it. That was the theme for the Eagles at this trade deadline. —Sheil Kapadia

Warning to NFL general managers: Howie Roseman is about to fleece you – NBCSP

A broken-down receiver, a washed-up guard and an underachieving defensive tackle walk into a bar. And Howie Roseman walks out with two 1st-round picks and three 2nd-round picks. If I were an NFL general manager, I wouldn’t even answer the phone when Howie calls. Because you’re going to get fleeced. And if there’s one thing to feel good about during this miserable season to nowhere, it’s the way Howie has stockpiled premium draft picks with a series of what sure seem like lopsided trades. It all started in June when Roseman shipped disgruntled and divisive A.J. Brown to the Patriots for a 1st-round pick in 2027 and a 5th-round pick in 2027.

The Broad Street Bandit – PHLY Eagles

Yesterday afternoon, my phone buzzed. A text from Howie Roseman. “I’ll fix this, promise you.” It came shortly after the news broke that Howie had traded Jordan Davis to Jacksonville for a first-round pick in 2027 and a second in 2029. I looked at the return and started laughing. The Broad Street Bandit had struck again. The greatest pickpocket in the National Football League. Somewhere in Jacksonville, James Gladstone, the Jags’ 35-year-old GM, is frantically checking his pants, wondering where his wallet went. Welcome to the world’s most expensive fantasy football contest, young man. In Reservoir Dogs, there was Mr. Pink and Mr. Blonde. And now the NFL has Mr. Fleece. Howie Roseman.

NFL trade deadline winners, losers: Vikings find QB, Jags go all-in, Jonathan Taylor stranded – The Athletic

Philadelphia Eagles. General manager Howie Roseman began his wheeling and dealing last month by trading center Cam Jurgens to the Baltimore Ravens for a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick. This week, Roseman couldn’t pass up the haul he received from the Jaguars for Davis. The Eagles now have 10 picks in the 2027 NFL Draft, highlighted by two first-rounders, a second, a third, a fourth, three fifths, a sixth and a seventh. Their 2028 haul features two firsts and seconds, as well as Philadelphia’s standard picks in rounds three through seven. In 2029, they have eight selections: a first-rounder, two seconds and one selection in each of the remaining rounds.

Eagles-Bengals trade canceled – BGN

The problem, however, is that Ebiketie was signed by the Eagles as a compensatory free agent, which means the Bengals would ultimately be giving up their comp pick from trading Trey Hendrickson during the offseason. So while on paper they were only trading a sixth-rounder, they really were giving up a third-round pick as well — notably, it’s interesting the Bengals hadn’t considered this factor before agreeing to terms…

The NFL’s 6 biggest disappointments so far – SB Nation

No. 6: Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles just suck. No way to sugarcoat it. While it’s true that Jalen Hurts’ injury really threw a wrench in things, the Eagles were mediocre before that happened. This was a team supposed to cruise to an easy NFC East championship, maybe have to contend with the Cowboys — and that was really it. Instead, they stepped on rakes for so long it busted their face, leaving them utterly incapable of playing effectively this season. Rotten from the top down, the only question remaining is whether or not Philadelphia has the guts to make some of the difficult choices needed in the offseason to get this team back on the right track.

Almost a Trade – Iggles Blitz

I really wanted them to move Riq Woolen so this is really frustrating. Moving Davis and adding the first and second round picks means this was a successful trade deadline for the Birds. It would have been nice to make another deal or two, but that would have been for late rounds picks. Those resources can help. They just aren’t nearly as impactful as first and second round picks. Howie made the most of a tough situation (the 2026 season).

The Philadelphia Eagles’ 2026 trade haul is likely to age well over time – ESPN

This is not exactly screaming quick fix. And with the futures of both offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and defensive coordinator Vic Fangio up in the air — not to mention the fate of coach Nick Sirianni — there’s a good chance some players on the current roster won’t be scheme fits for what comes next. (To that end, the decision to part with Davis now for such a strong return may look prescient should the Eagles shift to a defensive system that doesn’t value a run-stuffing nose tackle as highly.) With just two wins, the Eagles are in the throes of a season that feels similar to 2012 and 2020 when the bottom fell out and change and repair were needed. The outlook has been poor enough this season that the front office felt comfortable trading away of pair of starters in-season in Jurgens and Davis, the latter of which was a team captain. These are not waters the Eagles have found themselves swimming in much over the past couple of decades. But in the mess lay opportunity, and Roseman has found a way to capitalize on it.

Twitter bashes Bengals for fumbling Arnold Ebiketie trade over compensatory draft pick – Cincy Jungle

It would probably have been better if Cincinnati hadn’t made any move than attempting one and then having to pull the offer.

2026 NFL Trade Deadline: Grades for every team – PFF

Philadelphia Eagles: A-. It’s always tough to get a read on what Howie Roseman will do, and it would have been surprising if the league’s most forward-thinking general manager didn’t sell off at least one marquee player. Retrieving a first- and second-round pick for Davis, who owns the 24th-ranked overall PFF grade at his position, was outstanding. Yet Roseman also probably should have dealt pending free agents like Riq Woolen, Dallas Goedert and Arnold Ebiketie, if not considered trading major names like Zack Baun and Cooper DeJean.

Nick Sirianni denies giving subtle middle finger to fans – PFT

Frankly, what else would Sirianni say? “Yes, it was a middle finger.” If he admits it, he’ll be fined — and the precedent for coaches is $100,000. Beyond that, why would anyone believe him? Last Friday, Sirianni admitted that he misled reporters regarding the team’s supposed commitment to quarterback Tanner McKee.There’s one other relevant factor, based on my own personal experience. My dad used to use that exact same move, during periodic verbal household disagreements with my mom. I saw it. She never did. But that was the move. And, if she’d seen it, he would have denied it. Just like Sirianni did.

Jordan Davis modeled his game after John Henderson. Now he’s a Jaguar. – Big Cat Country

Through the first four and a half seasons of his pro career, Davis hasn’t panned out to be a Henderson clone. He’s collected 9.5 sacks and 86 solo tackles in 73 career games. Meanwhile, Henderson had 22 sacks and 245 solo tackles in his first 80 career games. Unfortunately, Henderson played long enough ago that I can’t use any advanced statistics to tell you why Big Jordan could still be the modern version of Big John. (For the record, Davis ranked fourth in run-stop win rate and run defense EPA among DTs last season.) Still, the comparison won’t end any time soon. Davis will be expected to help deliver the ring that long evaded Henderson, Marcus Stroud, DaVon Hamilton, and other DT franchise legends. Jacksonville has always been known for its standout running backs. Now that Davis is here, the defensive tackle position could be the bigger reason that the Jaguars are celebrated.

Dolphins move Malik Willis to IR – The Phinsider

Kyle McCord will move into the starting role for the 1-7 Dolphins. A 2025 sixth-round draft pick of the Philadelphia Eagles, McCord spent the preseason with the Green Bay Packers before Miami acquired him in a trade as final roster cuts were being made. After spending all of his rookie season on the Eagles’ practice squad, McCord will now make his NFL debut following the Willis injury.

Ravens trade G Andrew Vorhees to Falcons for C Ryan Neuzil – Baltimore Beatdown

This year, Neuzil started Atlanta’s first nine games with lower run-blocking grades but similar numbers in pass protection. He now seems headed for a backup role in Baltimore behind Cam Jurgens, who was acquired from the Philadelphia Eagles last month. The Ravens have been snakebitten by center injuries this year, and Jurgens has a history of back problems. Neuzil is a significant upgrade over Kyle Hergel, who took over the backup center job after Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic suffered long-term knee injuries in Week 3.

NY Giants trade deadline analysis: Nothing happened, and that’s OK – Big Blue View

The Giants? They are not there yet. Winning the NFC East would be a massive accomplishment. Remember, they won seven games combined the last two seasons. It would be a tremendous step in the right direction for a proud franchise that has been down for most of the last 15 years. I went on record a few days ago saying that I thought the Giants should make another run at Taylor, but that the price couldn’t be more than the second-round pick plus that they had already offered. Not giving away their first-round pick was the proper decision. In Harbaugh’s words, the prudent one. The Tennessee Titans did not want to trade running back Tony Pollard. He is a nice player, but Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy are nice players, too. The Giants could have used defensive tackle help. They were never getting Jeffery Simmons, and they weren’t foolish enough to give up a first-round pick for Davis. The Colts apparently wanted a fourth-round pick for Grover Stewart. The Giants didn’t have one to give. They do have Malachi Fields. They didn’t have a fifth-round pick. They do have J.J. McCarthy. Harbaugh had warned on Sunday that the Giants would protect their future.

Is the NFC East really winnable by the Cowboys? – Blogging The Boys

At 4-5, they trail the 5-2-1 New York Giants who are currently going through QB issues due to injury. The Giants keep winning by beating bad teams, something the Cowboys have not been as good at. The Cowboys wasted some of their soft schedule while the Giants mostly made good on theirs. So do you believe the Cowboys can win the NFC East and make the playoffs? The second half of the season gets harder for the Cowboys, but the same can be said of the Giants.

Commanders vs. Giants Tuesday injury report: Treylon Burks limited – Hogs Haven

Treylon Burks had a big Tuesday ahead. He needed to work and show the Commanders that he can play again. This was a big practice, and, honestly, the only one where the veteran receiver could prove worthy of playing in Thursday’s game against the New York Giants. Are we sure he’s going to go? We are not. But there’s some hope after he was considered limited on the Commanders’ official injury report.

item.title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers stand pat at trade deadline
item.description: No trades in Green Bay. Is that okay?
item.content:encoded:
The Packers, more or less as expected, didn’t do anything at this year’s edition of the NFL trade deadline.

Reportedly, it wasn’t for lack of trying. The Packers apparently had an offer on the table for Indianapolis Colts defensive lineman Grover Stewart, but the Colts dragged their feet and the Packers moved on, content to stand pat with what they have (which includes a couple of options still yet to return from injured reserve).

Time will tell whether they made the right moves. Or, rather, didn’t make the wrong moves. Or maybe made the right move by not making any moves at all. But I still sense an undercurrent of frustration among some fans and writers.

To be sure, there’s a point to some of the criticism. The Packers do have needs. They could stand to get better at running back and on the offensive line. They’re not exactly awash in defensive line options.

But having needs doesn’t mean you can just go fill them at the drop of your hat. What if nobody wants to trade you an offensive lineman? What if the cost to get a running back is prohibitive? What if the Colts decide to just hang on to a guy who’s going to be a free agent in the spring anyway?

I’ve never done it, but I’m told it takes two to tango. That’s true in the trade market as well, and arguably you might need at least three: a GM in Green Bay willing to deal, a prospect worth acquiring, and an opposing GM willing to play ball. The Packers have at least one of those and may have had two, but couldn’t find a dance partner. Them’s the breaks sometimes.

Perhaps more to the point, I don’t know if any trade the Packers could have made would have solved what ails them. Put Jonathan Taylor behind this offensive line and you probably get better performance than the Packers have had from the position so far, but also a worse version of what you’d probably expect from Taylor. Outside of Quenton Nelson, I don’t know if a single offensive lineman fixes much. The best move might have been a defensive lineman, but, again, you can’t trade for what nobody wants to give you.

item.title: Raiders ended up buying a third-round pick for $650,000
item.description: Did the Raiders get enough for Kirk Cousins?
item.content:encoded:
Did the Raiders get enough for Kirk Cousins?

Some will say no, because the Vikings were desperate to find a quarterback after Monday night's disastrous performance from Carson Wentz. They clearly have no faith in Kyler Murray, and they weren't ready to hand the reins to Max Brosmer. The Raiders had leverage, and it's fair to wonder whether they maximized.

But there's another reality to consider. The Vikings were casting a wide net. They apparently had other options. So if the Raiders had tried to put their thumb on the scale, the Vikings would have gone to a different deli — and the Raiders would have gotten nothing.

They were obviously going to pivot from Cousins to Fernando Mendoza at some point. Possibly, after the Week 13 bye against the Chargers. So they accelerated the plan and got something when they otherwise would have gotten nothing.

Along the way, they avoided the $10 million guaranteed 2027 roster bonus that was engineered to stick the Falcons with $8.7 million of Cousins's $10 million pay for 2026. In the end, the Raiders paid half of Cousins's $1.3 million base salary.

Setting aside the fact that they got nine games out of Cousins (including four wins) and a great mentor for Mendoza, the Raiders ultimately bought a third-round pick for $650,000.

In 2017, the Browns bought a second-round pick from the Texans for $16 million, in the form of taking on Brock Osweiler's remaining salary guarantee under a contract Houston quickly regretted. If a second-round pick was worth $16 million then, how much is a third-round pick worth now?

Whatever it is, it's more than $650,000.

So it was a win for the Raiders. And it was a win for the Vikings.

It also was a win for Cousins, who'll now be the starter for the rest of the season in Minnesota, without having to worry about getting benched for Murray, Wentz, or Brosmer.

item.title: Have the Saints finally cleaned up their discipline issues?
item.description: New Orleans showed progress after the bye, but one game isn't enough to tell if the penalty problem is fixed.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints have spent much of the season making life harder on themselves with costly penalties. Whether it’s been extending opposing drives, putting the offense behind the chains or simply failing to execute when it matters most, discipline has been a consistent concern.

However, Sunday’s win over the Cleveland Browns gave fans a reason to believe things might finally be moving in the right direction.

The Saints finished the day with just four penalties for 25 yards, a big improvement from what we’ve seen throughout the first half of the season. The Saints have struggled to avoid those self-inflicted setbacks, making Sunday’s performance a refreshing change.

Coming out of the bye week, there was an opportunity for Kellen Moore, his coaching staff and the players to address some of the issues that have held them back.

Still, it would be an overreaction to say the Saints have officially solved their problems.

One game, regardless of how encouraging it was, doesn’t take back the mistakes that have continued to show up throughout the first half of the season. Consistency is key in the NFL, and it’s beyond time for Kellen Moore and New Orleans to prove they can maintain this level of discipline moving forward.

The encouraging part is that the Saints showed they are capable of playing a much cleaner game.

It’s too early to say the issue fixed, but it is certainly fair to believe the bye week helped to some degree.

Now the challenge is making Sunday’s discipline the expectation rather than the exception.

item.content:encoded:
Week 9 of the NFL season is in the books. Here’s how it looked from an NFLSU perspective.

Jaguars 33 @ Ravens 10

The only former Tiger to play in this game was Jaguars WR Brian Thomas Jr. Despite playing 19 offensive snaps, he never got a target.

Grade: F

Bengals 34 vs* Falcons 17 (Madrid)

For the Falcons, DE Maason Smith recorded a QB hit and LB Harold Perkins Jr. had three tackles (two solo) including a TFL. For the Bengals, oh my goodness. QB Joe Burrow went 24/29 for 271 yards and 3 TDs for a QBR of 140.1 through the air. He also added three rushes for 7 yards and another TD. WR Ja’Marr Chase caught 10 of his 12 targets for 155 yards and 1 gorgeous 47-yard TD. He also set a franchise record with 142 yards in the first half. This was incredible.

Grade: A+

This game means everything.

While a win won’t ensure anything, it would at least give Washington a chance moving forward. A loss, however, would make the team’s road to the playoffs [effectively impossible].

After the Giants lost star outside linebacker Brian Burns to a torn ACL in Week 3, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson…turned up the heat. Since Week 4, New York’s defense has blitzed opponents on 46.5 percent of their dropbacks (second-highest rate in the NFL). Wilson hasn’t blitzed anyone more than he did the Commanders in Week 5. They blitzed on 62.2 percent of Washington’s dropbacks and sacked quarterback Jayden Daniels five times.

The Giants had a season-high seven sacks in their win over the Eagles. Although they have a talented defensive line, their most effective pass rusher has been inside linebacker Arvell Reese, who had three sacks against Philadelphia.

As the Commanders attempt to curb New York’s aggression, they will have to do so with a backup at center. Starting center Lucas Patrick suffered a concussion against the Rams and won’t be able to clear concussion protocol by Thursday. Veteran Nick Allegretti will start in his place against the Giants.

Commanders Film Review: Defending Puka Nacua

The Washington Commanders defense played relatively well in the loss to the LA Rams on Sunday. But the Rams are dealing with a lot of injuries on offense and only really had one receiving threat in this game, star receiver Puka Nacua. So it’s fair to ask if the Rams only really had one receiving threat in this game, how did the Commanders allow Nacua to be so productive? Surely you just double up on Nacua and stop the ball going his way and make others beat you? Well, it’s not quite that simple unfortunately. For starters, the Rams did a great job moving him around and forcing the ball to him. Four of his 14 catches were on receiver screens, for example.

There’s not really any way to stop a team throwing receiver screens if that’s the way they want to force the ball to their star receiver. You’ll notice that on three of those four plays, the Commanders were in a blitz look with multiple extra defenders walked up on the line of scrimmage. Those quick screens to Nacua were clearly a game plan option for the Rams to try and help deal with the Commanders tendency to load the box and send aggressive blitzes.

Ultimately, the Commanders did a pretty good job on these. Nacua gained some yards, but the first screen came on third and eight, Nacua only got six so the Commanders forced a fourth down. The second screen saw K’Lavon Chaisson punch the ball out and Nick Cross recover the fumble. The third screen came on third and 10 and Chaisson chased down Nacua to keep the gain to seven yards, again forcing another fourth down. It was only really the final one that did damage and that was just eight yards on first and 10, so that’s not the end of the world either.

But that’s only four of Nacua’s 10 catches, so what happened on the rest. Well, there was a good mix of plays where the Commanders actually had pretty solid coverage and Matthew Stafford made a great throw or Nacua made a great catch. There were also a few plays where I think the Commanders would like to have done a better job. item.title: The Chiefs’ pass rush came alive against the Jets
item.description: A closer look at how well Kansas City’s pass rush played in Sunday’s victory over New York.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs defeated the New York Jets 35-12 on Sunday, improving to a 6-2 record. While the game was close early on, timely red-zone defense and a dominant second half kept the Jets out of the end zone and held them scoreless.

A big factor in the performance was the pass rush. Leading up to the game, the Chiefs’ pass rush failed to make any meaningful impact in the losses to the Seattle Seahawks and the Denver Broncos. After being called out this week for the lack of production, the defensive line showed up and played their best game since the opener.

Here is how they did it

Chris Jones returns to form

The Chiefs’ All-Pro defensive tackle has had a slow start to the season, but he exploded for his best game of the year on Sunday, recording two sacks and creating pressure throughout.

Early on, Jones applied quick pressure using power rushes, setting the table for his counter moves later in the game.

Jones still has the power to move opposing linemen at will when left single-blocked, and this week he made Geno Smith uncomfortable by crushing the pocket early in the game.

The power moves are designed to put offensive linemen on skates and force them into overaggression off the snap, which is when he can work his counters like his hand swipe-to-rip combo.

Throughout his career, this has been Jones’s go-to move. On the snap, the right guard tries to set quick on Jones and gets his hands on him first to stop the power rush. Jones lined up with a running start from his alignment in front of the tackle, took advantage of the guard’s flat set, and swatted his hands away while ripping through the B-gap. The guard’s quick set means he didn’t get much depth, which gives Jones a very quick path to the quarterback.

Jones interior pass rush was good all game, but later on he had his best rush of the season from the edge.

At this stage in his career, Jones does not have the same explosion and quickness that he did to beat tackles off the edge consistently as he did in years prior, but as shown with his sack of the right tackle, he can still load up and bring his full force and quickness for one play in late-game situations.

It’s not a spot the Chiefs should line him up in frequently at this stage in his career, but it is a good curveball for them to throw in late-game situations.

Karlaftis continues playing well

Arguably the Chiefs’ best defensive player so far this season, defensive end George Karlaftis continued his strong season on Sunday, finishing good pass-rush attempts with sacks.

His effort and hustle on a game-in, game-out basis are undeniable, but the main criticism of his game has been his failure to finish plays with sacks.

Before the Chiefs’ Week 5 bye, Karlaftis did not record a sack, but since then he has recorded four, including two on Sunday.

On the snap, Karlaftis lands inside with his hands on the right tackle and walks him into the pocket. He gets to the quarterback’s level, disengages the block, and engulfs him for a sack.

Karlaftis has used the bull rush a few times this season to compress tackles into the pocket, and he is playing with more power than he has shown so far in his career.

A relentless motor and good timing also helped him collect another sack.

The Jets sell a play-action look off the snap, which makes Karlaftis hesitate out of the gate initially. As the quarterback pulls the ball, Karlaftis gets a bead on the play and quickly accelerates around the tackle. Sensing danger and under duress from rookie edge R Mason Thomas, the quarterback attempts to flee, but Karlaftis bends and gets just enough of his ankles to bring him down for a sack.

Ashton Gillotte

Getting in on the sack party was second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte, who had his best game as a pro rushing the passer.

Finishing with five pressures and one sack, Gillotte strung together a well-deserved performance getting after the quarterback.

One of the Chiefs better run-stuffing defensive linemen this season, Gillotte found himself on the field when the Jets would try a trick play.

The Jets sell a duo look on the snap, but the running back quickly flips the ball back to the quarterback, who surveys down the field. Lined up as a 6-technique off the snap, Gillotte is solo-blocked by a tight end, but uses a fierce start off the line of scrimmage to drive him off the line. Recognizing the trick play, he uses a long arm to help disengage, and then hustles to attack the quarterback.

His sack came as the offense was preoccupied with Jones and Karlaftis.

With six defenders on the line, Gillotte inside, with Karlaftis as a 4-technique, and Jones a wide 5-technique, the Jets slide protection to the right. Jones loops inside while Karlaftis attacks the right B-gap. This causes the right guard to take Karlaftis, but the center lets Gillotte go with Jones looping.

The trap was set, and Gillotte quickly runs down the quarterback.

The bottom line

This is the kind of performance the Chiefs should expect from Jones and Karlaftis. They are the two highest-paid defensive players on the team, and as seen in Gillotte’s big game, they need to open up looks for the rest of their teammates.

Smith has been one of the most sacked quarterbacks so far this season, so this isn’t a game the defensive line can rest on; they should use it as a building block for where they want to go this season.

item.title: Rams cited as potential Brandon Aiyuk destination
item.description: The Rams need to do whatever they can to find receiver help
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams need to at least check in on wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk if the San Francisco 49ers release him, which seems like an inevitability. Aiyuk is not necessarily a transformative player after being out of football for so long, but after inactivity at the NFL trade deadline, the Rams need to find some way to boost a position group that’s currently in dire straits.

SI’s Grant Cohn named the Rams as a potential destination for Aiyuk:

Davante Adams is on Injured Reserve with a torn hamstring, and Puka Nacua is expected to be placed on IR after he recently suffered MCL, PCL and turf-toe injuries. So the Rams are desperate. And Aiyuk would be cheap. And he probably would be their No. 1 wide receiver until Nacua and Adams return. And nothing would make Aiyuk happier than to face the 49ers at some point this season. Keep in mind, the 49ers and Rams are scheduled to meet at Levi’s Stadium on December 13.

Puka Nacua is on injured reserve. Adams is as well. Now Jordan Whittington will miss time. Quarterback Matthew Stafford is running out of options at wide receiver, so it behooves Los Angeles to be aggressive with what’s left on the free agent market.

Brandon Aiyuk timeline

Aiyuk’s dramatic saga with the 49ers has ben well-publicized. After an All-Pro season in 2023, Aiyuk held out until signing a four-year, $120 million deal ahead of the 2024 campaign. His production dropped off and then he suffered a season-ending injury after playing just seven games. From then on, he refused to report back to the team and has been out of the sport for the better part of two years, while Kyle Shanahan has been dismissive at best about his former starter.

This ordeal could be close to an end, however, with Aiyuk applying for reinstatement and passing a physical this week.

Rams wide receiver needs

It took Aiyuk a few seasons to take off in San Francisco, but his breakout campaign was stellar, posting 75 catches for 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns. That was in 2023, which by NFL standards is an eternity, but anything close to that ceiling would be a boon for L.A.’s offense.

At his best, he’s a strong route runner and separator with a knack for gaining yards after the catch. He’s also a willing and able blocker on the boundary, which would assist an already excellent Rams rushing attack.

Clearly, he comes with sizable off-field baggage, but that feels like a secondary concern at this point.

Meanwhile, with Whittington hitting IR, the Rams’ subsequent move was to sign Xavier Smith back to the active roster, which adds back a player with experience on this team but not exactly one who strikes fear in opponents’ hearts. That leaves the Rams with a wide receiver corps of Smith, Tutu Atwell, C.J. Daniels and Konata Mumpfield. That’s just not a good enough group for a Super Bowl contender, which is exactly why there were so many receiver-related rumors swirling around the Rams for weeks heading into the trade deadline.

There are a handful of other veteran free agent wide receivers available right now, although none have the kind of ceiling that Aiyuk has. Maybe Darius Slayton or Curtis Samuel gets a call from Les Sneed instead in the coming days.

But if you’re going to take a shot at adding some kind of additional talent to the wide receivers room, you may as well go for broke with Brandon Aiyuk. It’s not the most exciting addition Los Angeles could make, but there’s only so much it can do with the trade deadline in the past and a slate of daunting games coming up down the stretch.

item.title: Steelers mid-season awards: Defensive Player of the Year
item.description: Steelers mid-season awards: Who wins Defensive Player of the Year?
item.content:encoded:
We are halfway through our Pittsburgh Steelers midseason awards, with MVP and Offensive Player of the Year both going to Jaylen Warren. Well, this will be an award the star running back can’t win, because today we are handing out our mid-season Defensive Player of the Year. Let’s dive in.

Ryan Parish – EDGE T.J. Watt: This was a tough one. Patrick Graham has this unit playing well and it’s stronger as a collective rather than one player outshining the rest. Cases could be made for Cam Heyward, Keeanu Benton, Jalen Ramsey, Patrick Queen or even Payton Wilson. But Watt and his 7.5 sacks are the splashiest, and his return to form this season has been a joy to watch.

Ryland Bickley – EDGE T.J. Watt: It’s tempting to get creative here: Jamel Dean essentially won the Steelers the Buccaneers game and has been essential in keeping the secondary alive without Joey Porter Jr. Keeanu Benton and Cam Heyward have led a dominating defensive line. But at the time of writing, Watt is tied for the NFL lead in sacks at midseason and continues to draw plenty of attention to open up opportunities for the rest of the front seven.

Joey Bray – EDGE T.J. Watt: Much like Ryan and Ryland, I want to branch out here, but Watt is the easy choice here. The Steelers unit is well on their way to being a top 10 scoring defense for the first time since 2023. Watt is the leader of it all, ties for the league lead in sacks through eight weeks. 

Austin Bechtold – EDGE T.J. Watt: Watt already has more sacks through eight games as he did in 14 last year. He recorded his first career pick-six against the Falcons and has benefitted from a reduced snap count. Patrick Graham is keeping Watt fresh with his usage and while you’d want Watt out there for as many snaps as possible, it’s working well. Watt looks like himself again.

Mike Nicastro – EDGE T.J. Watt: There are several worthy candidates on Pittsburgh’s defense, including Jalen Ramsey, Keeanu Benton and Cameron Heyward. However, my vote goes to the player who continues to set the standard for the Steelers’ defense: T.J. Watt. Watt has been a consistent disruptive force and has made his presence felt under defensive coordinator Patrick Graham. When he’s on the field, opposing offenses have to account for him on virtually every passing down.

Jason Aponte – EDGE T.J. Watt: Who else? Alex Highsmith has been excellent this season, but 7.5 sacks for Watt, with some game-breaking plays, push him to the top of the list. With 25 pressures, 14 hurries, three QB hits, and 19 pressures in true pass sets, to go with five sacks, 12 hurries, and two QB hits, Watt remains a force for the defensive line.

Jarrett Bailey – EDGE T.J. Watt: Yeah, we’re all going chalk here. Watt has turned back the clock, as he was tied for the league lead in sacks going into the Steelers’ bye week. He’s already topped his 2025 season total in sacks, and he is back to being the disruptive player that made him a Defensive Player of the Year Award winner. It’s been great to see No. 90 look like himself again.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Vikes Views: Kirk to the Rescue?
item.description: This is certainly not an article I expected to write at the start of the season. However, the Vikings’ trade for Kirk Cousins makes all the sense in the world. The Las Vegas Raiders appear ready to see what they have in former No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza, while the Minnesota Vikings have somehow […]
item.content:encoded:
This is certainly not an article I expected to write at the start of the season. However, the Vikings’ trade for Kirk Cousins makes all the sense in the world.

The Las Vegas Raiders appear ready to see what they have in former No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza, while the Minnesota Vikings have somehow scraped together a 6-2 record behind a dominant defense, excellent special teams, and one of the worst offenses in football.

The Vikings aren’t going to suddenly become an offensive juggernaut because of this move, but Cousins gives them something they haven’t had all season: competency at quarterback. The running game has struggled, in part because opposing defenses haven’t respected the passing attack.

Minnesota ranks second-to-last in the NFL at just 160.8 passing yards per game. Meanwhile, Cousins is averaging more than 260 passing yards and two touchdowns per game, though he is also averaging more than one turnover. The Raiders’ four wins have come against the Dolphins, Chargers, Saints, and Jets. They played the Chiefs and Bills tough, but were blown out by the Rams, 49ers, and Patriots. The numbers suggest Cousins can still function as a capable NFL starter, even if he’s no longer the player he was at his peak.

None of this guarantees success. The pessimist in me remembers the Randy Moss reunion and a long history of veteran acquisitions that failed to meet expectations. Midseason additions rarely transform teams into Super Bowl contenders.

That said, it’s absolutely the right move to make. This defense deserves better than what it has received from the offense through the first half of the season.. I’m not ready to declare them Super Bowl contenders just yet, but they win on Sunday, I might be. Nothing would be more Minnesota than to win the Super Bowl with an enigma of a quarterback like Kirk Cousins.

item.title: NFL trade deadline, odds: 3 bets that I like right now, including Fernando Mendoza to win Rookie of the Year
item.description: Our NFL handicapper gives three bets he likes after the NFL trade deadline.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL trade deadline was on Tuesday, and it sure was busy. There have been 18 completed trades since the start of the regular season, which included 23 of the 32 teams and 34 total draft picks changing hands (tied for the fourth most in the last 35 years).

QB Kirk Cousins going from the Las Vegas Raiders to the Minnesota Vikings to instantly supplant Carson Wentz and/or Kyler Murray as the team's starter was one of the biggest moves. The Jacksonville Jaguars were the most active buyers, bringing in multiple defensive starters, while the Indianapolis Colts offloaded multiple pieces for future draft capital.

As a bettor, my focus is instantly looking at the Week 10 games and futures market for value that ripples as an effect of these transactions. Usually the Week 10 games will see very quick market moves, but the futures market is a derivative place to attack for excellent post-trade deadline value.

Here are three futures worth placing now as it relates to the NFL trade deadline passing yesterday.

Los Angeles Rams to miss the playoffs (-118)

The Rams were in an incredibly difficult position at the trade deadline and were unable to get anything done. On the final offensive snap of their Week 9 win over the Washington Commanders, star WR Puka Nacua injured his right knee. He is now expected to miss several weeks, even if he doesn't land on injured reserve. WR Davante Adams is already on injury reserve, and so is their best pass-catching tight end Terrence Ferguson.

The Rams went from not needing to make a move to desperately hoping to add a wide receiver. They were unable to get anything done, which puts this team in a precarious situation over its final eight games.

If the season ended today, the 5-4 Rams would not be in the playoffs. The 49ers own the NFC West division and the Rams' record is not good enough to be a wild-card team. Based on the health of the team, it's going to be hard to play catch up. The offensive firepower is significantly compared to preseason expectations, and in this case not getting a deal done becomes a worst-case scenario as the WR room now hinges on Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell and CJ Daniels. On a day that saw Keenan Allen and Josh Downs get traded from Indianapolis, it's difficult for Rams fans to know neither ended up in Los Angeles.

I am taking a small victory lap because one of my preseason NFL futures was Rams to miss the playoffs at +400, and now it is still a good take at -118. If you already bet it, you can add onto it small and bet it again.

Philadelphia Eagles under 4.5 wins (+110)

The Eagles are on their bye this upcoming weekend, so the best way to react to Philadelphia trading defensive tackle Jordan Davis is by looking at the season wins market. In the 18 total trades made this NFL season, the Eagles trading Jordan Davis was one of two transactions to include a first-round pick. That shows you the level of star power that just left the Philadelphia franchise and headed to Jacksonville.

The soft tank is on in Philadelphia. This team has lost seven straight games and they are without QB Jalen Hurts for the rest of the season. After turning to Tanner McKee at QB after Hurts' injury news broke, they quickly stopped that experiment, signed Joe Milton off the Cowboys practice squad and he is now starting. I truly think the Eagles know this season is lost, they don't want to win and prefer to prioritize upcoming draft capital. In the NFL, the draft order is a direct reflection of the standings and the worse you do that season, the better your picks are.

The Eagles have a very forward-thinking front office. One reason they were able to get a first-round pick for Davis was because of his team-friendly contract. Davis was given a huge signing bonus when Philadelphia inked his deal, and thus his annual salary was lower and his trade value was higher. Those little edges the Eagles gain are indirect ways to show they will prioritize next season over squeezing out an extra win or two.

I expect Milton to remain the starter and players that are injured — like DeVonta Smith with a hamstring issue — to be kept out as long as possible. An injury that a player might have played through on a contending team will now be a reason to sit out.

I am betting the Eagles regular-season win total under 4.5, hoping they don't win three of their final eight games.

Fernando Mendoza to win Offensive Rookie of the Year (+300)

Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick in the 2026 NFL draft, has been announced as the Raiders starting QB with Cousins' departure. Mendoza is primed to make a run for Offensive Rookie of the Year over the second half of the season. His head coach is Klint Kubiak, who was the offensive coordinator of the Super Bowl-winning Seattle Seahawks last season. Mendoza has the best pass-catching tight end in Brock Bowers to target. And of course, we can expect Raiders owner Tom Brady to be speaking with Mendoza regularly the rest of the season as well.

The other side of this is looking at Mendoza's competition for this award.

There have been no standout players who are leading the pack for OROY. The weak player pool here is why Mendoza now has the shortest odds simply by being named the starter. Broncos rookie RB Jonah Coleman and Titans WR Carnell Tate round out the top three with the shortest odds. Coleman had a stint on IR and is just now taking over the Broncos backfield. Tate just missed the last Titans game with his own injury and is in a crowded room of skill players in Tennessee.

Fourth and fifth in the odds are Cleveland Browns wideouts Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, each of whom takes away from the other's upside to win this award.

It seems like chalk, but going for the ceiling outcome on Mendoza's rest of season is worth playing into at 3-to-1 odds.

item.title: Browns roster: 4 moves after trade deadline, including bringing back 2 familiar names
item.description: The Cleveland Browns roster saw a few changes after the NFL trade deadline, including TE Zaire Mitchell-Paden’s return
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns roster did not see any major changes at the NFL trade deadline, and surprisingly few changes since the initial 53-man roster came out, but GM Andrew Berry kept making moves following the deadline. As previously reported, the Browns brought back TE Zaire Mitchell-Paden to the team’s practice squad.

Mitchell-Paden has only played in eight career games, six with the Baltimore Ravens and two with the New Orleans Saints in 2025, after entering the league as an undrafted free agent with Cleveland in 2022. The 6’5”, 257-pound tight end played at Notre Dame, Ohio, and Florida Atlantic in college and has caught two passes for 17 yards so far in his career.

The Browns also brought back punter Wes Pahl to the practice squad, again, despite Corey Bojorquez seemingly having a great year.

To make room for Mitchell-Paden and Pahl, Cleveland released TE John FitzPatrick and DT Eric Johnson II from their practice squad.
